docs.title: xdfem2D
docs.text:
xdfem2D is a 2D finite-element structural analysis application — frames, walls, slabs and grillages — pairing a Python analysis library (xdfem2d) with a PySide6 desktop interface for building models, running analyses, and reviewing results interactively.

Units throughout are kN · m · kNm.

docs.title: Two domains, one model type
docs.text: Every model is either plane (a frame or wall in its own plane) or plate (a slab or grillage bending out of plane) — chosen once, in New model, and fixed for the model's life. The two share the same solver machinery but mean different things element by element: see Domains (plane vs plate) for the full comparison, and Slabs and Grillages for a plate-focused walkthrough.

docs.title: Elements & modelling
docs.text:
• Plane: Euler–Bernoulli beam–column elements (full 6-DOF, 3 per node) and membrane triangles (CST / Allman / ES-FEM) for walls and panels, with automatic Delaunay meshing of polygon surfaces.
  • Plate: grillage beams (bending + St-Venant torsion) and plate-bending triangles — MITC3 (shear-deformable, thin and thick slabs) and DKT (thin-plate).
  • Pinned, roller, fixed, guided and rotational supports (plane) or their plate equivalents (simple, clamped, symmetry); node springs and element foundation (Winkler) springs, including tension-only / compression-only (unilateral) springs.
  • Parametric geometry (arcs, polylines) that auto-resolves T-junctions and crossings, plus automatic topology checks (isolated/coincident nodes, unconnected junctions, duplicate bars).

docs.title: Loads & analysis
docs.text:
• Point loads, trapezoidal distributed loads, thermal loads, support settlements, nodal masses, self-weight by load-case factor, and — in the plate domain — area pressure and Winkler area springs (slab on grade).
  • A clear three-tier model — load cases (define loads) → analysis cases (solve them) → combinations (combine analysis cases) — mirroring the convention used by mainstream structural software.
  • Analysis types: Linear, NonLinear (unilateral springs, active-set iteration), Mass, Modal (eigenvalue), Response Spectrum (EC8), and Geometric Nonlinear (P-Delta) — the last two available in the plane domain.
  • Load combinations: linear, envelope (max/min), SRSS, and automatic Eurocode (EC0) combination generation.

docs.title: Structural design
docs.text:
• Concrete — EC2: reinforcement design (flexure + shear) for rectangular sections, EC2 crack-width (SLS) verification, and punching shear.
  • Steel — EC3: cross-section resistance and member buckling checks.
  • Timber — EC5: ULS member checks.
  • Slabs: Wood–Armer design moments reported per triangle, ready for an EC2 slab check.
  • EC8 seismic response spectra (elastic and design).

docs.title: Variants, phasing & interoperability
docs.text:
• Variants: parallel what-if scenarios over a shared model, combined with the same arithmetic as load combinations.
  • Construction phasing: incremental analysis carrying forward locked-in internal forces from earlier phases.
  • Import/export DXF, import/export SAP2000 (.s2k), and export to Autodesk Robot (.str).

docs.title: Interface & results
docs.text:
• Interactive canvas: cursor-anchored zoom, pan, window selection, hover tooltips, and named Scenes (saved working subsets of the model).
  • Parametric templates (portal frame, continuous beam, frame, Warren/Howe/ Pratt trusses, parabolic arch) to start a model in seconds.
  • An optional AI Assistant panel that answers questions about the open model in plain language — local by default (via Ollama), or a remote model with your own API key. See The AI Assistant.
  • Results: displacements, reactions, element end-forces, N/V/M diagrams, deformed and modal shapes, membrane stresses / slab moments, and reaction sums.
  • Exports: drawing (PNG/SVG/PDF), a formatted PDF results report, an Excel workbook (model or results), and Word reports.

docs.title: How the pieces fit together
docs.text:
Load case      →   Analysis case      →   Combination
(defines loads)    (solves the model)     (combines analysis cases)

This mirrors the convention used by mainstream structural software: a load case is only a definition of loads; it is an analysis case that actually gets solved, and combinations operate on analysis cases. See Analysis for the full picture.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Starting a new model? Read Domains (plane vs plate) first — it's the one choice you can't change later.
  • New here? Read Installation then Getting Started.
  • Want a tour of the windows and controls? See The Interface.
  • Building a model? See Modelling and Loads.
  • Running and reviewing analyses? See Analysis and Results.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
xdfem2D uses a three-tier model. Keeping these distinct is the key to using the program correctly.

Load case        Analysis case            Combination
──────────       ─────────────            ───────────
defines loads →  applies load cases   →   combines analysis cases
(no results)     with factors & a         (linear / envelope / SRSS / seismic)
                 solution method
                 (produces results)
  • Load case — a named set of loads. It is only a definition; on its own it produces no results.
  • Analysis case — references one or more load cases with factors and a solution method, and is solved. This is where results come from.
  • Combination — combines analysis cases (never load cases directly).

Automatic Linear cases

Adding a load case creates a Linear analysis case of the same name. If you build a combination that needs a load case directly, xdfem2D wraps that load case in a Linear analysis case automatically, so combinations always combine analysis cases.

docs.title: Analysis cases
docs.text:
Create them on the Analysis Cases sub-tab. Each type has its own form:

Type Purpose Key inputs Linear Static linear-elastic solution load-case coefficients; optional stored stiffness from a P-Delta run NonLinear Static solution honouring unilateral (tension-/compression-only) springs load-case coefficients (same inputs as Linear) Mass Build a mass matrix from gravity loads and/or nodal masses load-case→mass factors (e.g. G + 0.3·Q); concentrated nodal masses Modal Eigenvalue analysis number of modes; the Mass case to use Spectrum Response-spectrum analysis Modal case; spectral function; combination rule (SRSS/CQC); direction; damping Geometric Nonlinear P-Delta / large displacement method; max iterations; tolerance; member stiffness factors; load-case coefficients Sequence Incremental staged-construction analysis defined by a construction sequence (see Variants & Construction Sequences); appears automatically when a sequence is created

A Linear case may reuse the tangent stiffness of a Geometric Nonlinear (P-Delta) run instead of the elastic stiffness.

In the plate domain

Linear, non-linear static, modal and response-spectrum analysis are all available for slabs and grillages. The mass sits on the transverse DOF w, so the modes are the out-of-plane (vertical) vibration and the response spectrum is vertical. P-Delta is not available — its geometric stiffness is built from in-plane axial force, which a plate model does not carry. See Slabs and Grillages.

docs.title: NonLinear cases (unilateral springs)
docs.text:
A NonLinear case takes exactly the same inputs as a Linear case (load-case coefficients) but solves the model honouring tension-only / compression-only springs — see Springs. It is the only case type that activates that unilateral behaviour; in every other case type a spring acts bilaterally (resisting in both directions).

How it is solved: the case builds the combined load vector (Σ coeffᵢ · load caseᵢ) and runs an active-set iteration — each unilateral spring is included in the stiffness only while it is active (its displacement has the sign matching its mode), re-solving until the active set no longer changes. Because the result is non-linear, it cannot be scaled or superposed, which drives the combination rule below.

When a NonLinear case behaves like Linear

If the model has no tension-/compression-only springs, a NonLinear case produces exactly the same result as a Linear case.

docs.title: Mass and Modal cases
docs.text:
The mass matrix is diagonal (lumped): it is built from the absolute value of the vertical force |Fy|/g that each referenced load case puts on a node, plus any concentrated nodal mass. Two consequences are worth knowing before reading modal results:

  • the mass derived from a load case is applied equally to X and Y, so an upward load contributes the same mass as a downward one, and a purely horizontal load contributes no mass at all;
  • there is no rotary inertia unless a rotational nodal mass (mtz) is given explicitly.

Rocking modes need an explicit rotary inertia

Any mode whose kinematics involve the nodal rotations — the rocking of a rigid block on springs is the typical case — must be given a rotational mass mtz, otherwise it is carried by degrees of freedom that have no mass and are numerically regularised. The regularisation degrades the conditioning of the eigenproblem, and the resulting frequency can drift by several percent with the member stiffness and even between machines. For a member lumped into segments of length h, the consistent value is mtz = mᵢ·h²/12 at each node. With it, the same frequency is stable to 10⁻⁵.

Effective mass percentages are relative to the FREE mass

meff X % and meff Y % use as denominator the mass on the unrestrained degrees of freedom, reported as total_mass_x / total_mass_y. Mass lumped on a restrained DOF cannot vibrate — it goes straight to the foundation — so it is excluded. The denominator is chosen so that the percentages of all modes add up to 100 %, which makes the column a reliable indicator of mode truncation.

This is not the model's total mass. The results also carry model_mass_x / model_mass_y (everything, restrained included) and restrained_mass_x / restrained_mass_y, so the ratio against the total can be computed when needed — notably for the EC8 §4.3.3.3.1 criterion, which asks for 90 % of the total mass of the structure.

How much is excluded depends on the mesh, not on the structure: on a simply supported beam discretised into n elements the supported nodes carry exactly 1/n of the mass (6,3 % with 16 elements). Refining the mesh therefore moves the percentages even though the absolute effective masses converge. When the restrained fraction exceeds 2 %, the Modal case results include a warnings entry saying so.

Model check (Structure menu) additionally reports any concentrated nodal mass placed on a restrained DOF, since that is almost always a modelling slip rather than an intention.

docs.title: Response spectra (seismic)
docs.text:
A Spectrum analysis case reads a spectral function — a curve of spectral acceleration Sa(T) — and a referenced Modal case, then combines the modal responses (SRSS or CQC) in a chosen direction (X, Y, or XY). Define the spectral functions in Structure → Spectral Functions. You can build one three ways:

  • By code (EC8:2004) — pick Type 1 / Type 2, ground type A–E, the reference ground acceleration agR, importance factor γI and damping ξ. Choose Design (Sd) — which uses the behaviour factor q and the lower-bound factor β — or Elastic (Se). The soil parameters (S, TB, TC, TD) are derived and shown.
  • By national-annex zone — the same, driven by a seismicity zone that fixes agR.
  • User-defined — enter S, TB, TC, TD and ag directly, or a raw list of (T, Sa) points.

The response-spectrum result of a Spectrum case is the peak (absolute) response; when it enters a combination it becomes a seismic envelope (see below).

docs.title: Combinations
docs.text:
Create them on the Combinations sub-tab. A combination references analysis cases only — eligible members are Linear, NonLinear, P-Delta (Geometric Nonlinear), and Spectrum cases. Modal and Mass cases cannot be combined.

NonLinear cases in combinations

A non-linear result cannot be scaled or added to others, so a combination that references a NonLinear case may contain only that single case, with a combination factor of 1.0 — no other analysis cases of any type. xdfem2D rejects combinations that break this rule.

Combination types:

Type Rule SomaLinear Σ coeffᵢ · caseᵢ (signed linear superposition) Envolvente Envelope: max/min of each component across the weighted cases SomaModulo Σ |coeffᵢ · caseᵢ| (sum of absolutes) RaizSoma √(Σ (coeffᵢ · caseᵢ)²) (SRSS)

When a combination references a Spectrum case, the result becomes a seismic envelope: the gravity base ± Σ |coeffₛ · spectrumₛ|.

docs.title: Automatic Eurocode combinations
docs.text: Loads → Auto Comb. (EN 1990)… (Ctrl+Shift+C) generates ULS/SLS combinations from the load cases' action types. Generated combinations are folded into analysis-case references on the next refresh.

docs.title: Construction sequences
docs.text:
A Sequence analysis case represents an incremental staged-construction analysis. Each sequence is composed of ordered phases — each phase adds elements, applies load cases as an increment, and optionally changes the provisional support set. The solver carries locked-in forces forward from phase to phase, so later members do not attract load that earlier ones already resisted.

Sequence cases are created and edited in Analysis → Variants Workspace… on the Sequences tab. They appear in the case drop-down alongside normal cases and combinations (order: analysis cases → sequences → combinations), and their results are navigated phase by phase using the phase selector in the toolbar. See Variants & Construction Sequences for the full workflow.

docs.title: Running
docs.text: Press F5 or the Run button. Results lock the model; unlock with Ctrl+L to edit (which clears results). See Results.

docs.title: The AI Assistant
docs.text:
The AI panel answers questions about the open model in plain language: where the largest stress is, which combination governs the reinforcement, what a command does. Show or hide it from View → Assistant panel.

It is optional. Every other part of xdfem2D works without it, and the panel says so when nothing is installed.

docs.title: Local or remote
docs.text:
By default the assistant runs the model on your own machine through Ollama, and nothing about your structure leaves it.

If you have an API key, you can use the far more capable remote models from OpenAI, Google and others instead. They answer more reliably, are usually faster, and are noticeably better at building a model than a model that fits on a laptop. Press Providers… beside the model list, paste the key, and those models appear in the list below a separator, labelled with the provider.

docs.title: Other providers
docs.text:
Most services speak OpenAI's API at a different address, so OpenAI, Google Gemini, Ollama Cloud, DeepSeek, Kimi (Moonshot), GLM (Zhipu), Mistral, Groq and OpenRouter are already listed under Providers…. Paste a key beside one and its models join the list.

Anthropic is not among them: its API is shaped differently enough to need a second client library and a second translation of every tool, which is a lot of machinery — and a lot of megabytes in the packaged application — for one provider out of ten. Claude models are available through OpenRouter.

docs.title: Ollama somewhere else
docs.text:
Two different things, and only one of them sends your model away.

Ollama Cloud runs the models on Ollama's machines. Add an OLLAMA_API_KEY under Providers… and it behaves like any other remote service — same warning, same marking in the list. Useful on a laptop that cannot hold an 8B model.

Your own Ollama on another machine — an office workstation with a GPU, say — needs nothing here at all. The local provider follows Ollama's own OLLAMA_HOST variable:

export OLLAMA_HOST=http://workstation.local:11434

The panel then lists that machine's models and nothing leaves your network. For work under a confidentiality obligation this is the arrangement to prefer: the speed of a real GPU with none of the disclosure.

For anything else — a service newer than this release, or a company gateway — use Add endpoint… in the same dialog. It asks for a name and the base URL of the OpenAI-compatible API, and writes them to ~/.xdfem2d/llm_endpoints.json:

{
  "myprovider": {
    "env": "MYPROVIDER_API_KEY",
    "base_url": "https://api.example.com/v1",
    "models": ["some-model"]
  }
}

That file holds addresses, not secrets. An entry there overrides a built-in one, which is how to correct an address that has moved without waiting for a new release.

docs.title: Where the keys are kept
docs.text:
In your system keychain — Keychain Access on macOS, and the equivalent elsewhere — under the service name xdfem2d. They are encrypted at rest, and you can inspect or revoke them there without going through this application.

They are never written to the preferences file, which is plain text, and never into a .x2d, which would carry the key to whoever you send the model to.

An environment variable of the same name still works and is useful for scripting, but it is second in line: a key stored through the dialog wins. Note that launching from the Dock or Finder does not inherit shell variables, so a key set only in ~/.zshrc will appear missing — another reason to prefer the dialog.

Storing keys needs the keyring package, which ships with xdfem2D. It is not a vault of its own — on macOS it is a thin layer over the system Keychain, the same one Safari uses, and the entries appear in Keychain Access under the service name xdfem2d. The first time a key is saved, macOS asks whether Python may use the Keychain; answer Always Allow or it will ask again at every start.

If it is missing from your environment, install it with pip install keyring. The dialog says so rather than failing quietly, and falls back to environment variables meanwhile.

No extra install is needed for any of them. The openai client is a normal dependency of xdfem2D and ships with the packaged application, and every provider above is reached through it — only the key is missing.

Choosing one sends your model to a third party. The question, and whatever the assistant reads to answer it — geometry, loads, sections, results — goes over the internet. For work under a confidentiality obligation, that is a decision to make deliberately, not one to discover afterwards; the panel asks once per session before the first remote question. Remote models are faster and make none of the mistakes the local ones make, and neither fact changes the first sentence of this paragraph.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
The assistant talks to Ollama, which runs the language model on your own machine. Nothing about your model is sent anywhere.

  1. Install Ollama.
  2. Start it: ollama serve
  3. Fetch a model: ollama pull granite4.1:8b
  4. Press Refresh in the panel.

Neither Ollama nor the model ships with xdfem2D — the model alone is several gigabytes, and most installations never open this panel.

docs.title: Choosing a model
docs.text:
Two things matter, and neither is obvious from the model's name.

It must support tool calling. The assistant never guesses: it asks the application for the numbers through a set of query tools. A model that cannot call them will answer anyway, from nothing, and the invented stresses look exactly like real ones. The panel marks such models — no tool support.

Bigger is not a luxury here. This is the part worth reading twice. A smaller model answers faster and fits in less memory, so it looks like the sensible choice on a modest machine. It is not. In testing, a 3B model asked to locate the most stressed element named the right element, skipped the tool that knows where it is, and reported fabricated coordinates — adding that they were "derived from the element locations within the analysed mesh", which they were not. It did this in two runs out of five. The same model described required reinforcement as "the limit you must not exceed", inverting the meaning while quoting the correct figure.

A small model here does not give worse answers. It gives wrong answers that look exactly like right ones.

docs.title: Tested models
docs.text:
Measured with tools/bench_assistant.py, seven questions x five repetitions, July 2026:

Model Correct s/answer Notes granite4.1:8b 35/35 11 Recommended — nothing answers better, and nothing correct is faster. qwen3.5:9b 35/35 26* Equally reliable, well over twice as slow. gemma4:12b-mlx 35/35 36 Equally reliable, slower again. granite4.1:3b 32/35 5 Fabricated coordinates; inverted a design concept.

Three models answer every question correctly, so accuracy does not choose between them — speed does. Note that the smallest model is the fastest and the least trustworthy: the two are not in tension here, they are unrelated.

* measured before tool results were capped, a change that cut the others by about a quarter; treat it as an upper bound.

Times are from one machine. Without a usable GPU the same model can be several times slower.

These names will age. The benchmark will not: it computes the right answers from the model file itself, so it stays valid as models and files change.

PYTHONPATH=src python3 tools/bench_assistant.py yourfile.x2d a_model --runs=5

Rank by the stable column — questions answered correctly on every run. A model that is right four times in five is not one to compute with.

docs.title: A tool call that comes back as text
docs.text:
Occasionally a model — even one that generally supports tool calling — writes what looks like a tool call as plain text instead of actually making one: something like {"tool_calls": [...]} appears as the answer itself. The panel cannot act on that; it is not a real call, and the reply is marked "answered without consulting the model — treat any numbers as unverified".

This is not the application failing to recognise a valid call — it is the underlying runtime (Ollama) failing to recognise the model's output as one, because the model drifted slightly off the exact format its own chat template expects. It tends to happen more with smaller models, and not always on the same question twice.

The Temperature control, beside the Model output combo, is the knob for this. Lower (around 0.2) keeps the model closer to the format it was trained to reproduce exactly — steadier tool use, less varied wording. It does not make the drift impossible, only less likely; a model with no tool support at all will not gain any by turning this down. Default is 0.7.

docs.title: What it can and cannot do
docs.text:
It reads, and it can propose a new model. It cannot edit the currently open model in place, run the analysis, or write files directly.

It is given a short summary of the model up front and asks for detail through the tools, so it sees the geometry, loads, cases, results, nodal-averaged stresses, design results, constraints and this manual. Results are keyed to the analysed mesh — the elements that geometry objects expand into — and the assistant uses those ids, which is why they may not match what you drew.

docs.title: Creating a model
docs.text:
Ask it to build a structure — "a 6 m simply supported beam", "a cantilever wall", "a simply supported slab" — and it answers with a new model, written as JSON. The application checks it and, if it is complete, offers a button to open it; you never have to trust it blind. This is genuinely useful for a quick starting point, but treat it as early and limited:

  • it works from small templates — a beam (bars) or a wall (triangles) in the plane domain, or a slab (plate-bending triangles) or grillage (beam grid) in the plate domain — and edits their values; it is not a general modeller;
  • the more elaborate the request, the more likely something is missing or wrong, so review what opens before you build on it;
  • a capable model matters most here. A small local model often produces a structure that looks right and is not; a stronger remote model (with an API key) is markedly better both at answering and at building.

Open model applies a JSON model that opens cleanly right away — one click, same as before. One that does not open is opened instead in the same JSON editor described below, in place of just naming the problem — what stops one is usually a single wrong word, and the editor's Apply re-checks it after a fix, with no need to leave the application or hand-edit a saved file elsewhere.

It can also write a Python build script (using the xdfem2d API) when you ask for one instead of a model. A script never runs on its own: Open model loads it into the Script editor (Ctrl+Shift+E), and nothing happens to the current model until you press Run yourself. The editor's Save… button writes the text as it stands to a file (.py or .json), independently of applying it.

Two habits make it more useful:

  • Name the case. "In COMBO1" rather than "in the model": extremes differ between load cases and combinations, and the assistant will otherwise have to pick one and tell you which.
  • Check anything that matters. Use Edit → Find Entity to jump to an element it names, and confirm the number in the results table. The assistant is a way to find things quickly, not a substitute for reading the results.

Design values exist only for combinations that were actually designed. Ask about an analysis case and a good model will tell you there is nothing there.

docs.title: Plano de implementação de constraints (ligações cinemáticas) — xdfem2D
docs.text:
Estado: implementado (Fases 0–5, por penalização). Este documento é o plano original. As Fases 0 a 5 estão concluídas — modelo de dados, solver por penalização, persistência, validação (model_check), interface (painel, diálogo, canvas, menus) e assistente AI — mais a recuperação das forças de constraint (método do resíduo) e a documentação de utilizador em modelling.md / results.md. Fica por fazer, como previsto, a Fase 2 exata (transformação mestre–escravo) e o diafragma rígido.

Documento de planeamento. Descreve o modelo de dados, o motor de resolução, a serialização, a interface gráfica e a interação com o utilizador (incluindo o assistente AI) para acrescentar constraints ao xdfem2D.

docs.title: 1. O que são "constraints" aqui
docs.text:
Hoje o xdfem2D restringe graus de liberdade (DOF) de duas formas: Support (apoios — fixa um DOF a um valor, tipicamente zero ou um assentamento imposto) e NodeSpring/ElementSpring (molas — acrescentam rigidez a um DOF). Ambas atuam sobre um único DOF de cada vez.

Uma constraint (restrição de vínculo múltiplo, multi-point constraint — MPC) é diferente: relaciona vários DOFs entre si através de uma equação linear. Os casos que interessam a um pórtico 2D com 3 DOF por nó (ux, uy, tz):

  • Equal DOF / "body constraint" — obriga um conjunto de nós a partilhar o mesmo valor de um ou mais DOFs (ex.: uy igual em vários nós).
  • Rigid link (master–slave) — um nó "escravo" segue um nó "mestre" como se estivessem ligados por um corpo rígido: ux_s = ux_m − (y_s − y_m)·tz_m, uy_s = uy_m + (x_s − x_m)·tz_m, tz_s = tz_m. É a base de tudo o resto.
  • Rigid diaphragm (piso rígido) — caso especial do rigid link muito usado em edifícios: um conjunto de nós de um piso partilha o deslocamento horizontal e a rotação de um nó mestre do piso (translação transversal livre). Num modelo 2D reduz-se essencialmente a "mesmo ux + mesma rotação de corpo".
  • Equação de vínculo genérica — Σ cᵢ·dofᵢ = g, a forma mais geral, da qual todas as anteriores são casos particulares.

Recomendação de âmbito para a 1.ª versão: implementar a equação genérica como representação interna única e oferecer ao utilizador três atalhos de alto nível (Equal DOF, Rigid link, Rigid diaphragm) que geram essas equações. É o mesmo padrão que o projeto já usa com CANONICAL_SUPPORTS (nomes canónicos para combinações de restrições).

docs.title: 2. Estado atual relevante (levantamento)
docs.text:
O plano abaixo assenta no que existe hoje:

  • Numeração de DOF — Structure2D.node_dof_index (em structure.py, ~l.1537) atribui 3·i a cada nó, num_dofs = 3·n_nós. É invalidada (posta a None) sempre que a topologia muda. É o ponto único onde o mapa DOF é definido.
  • Assemblagem — assembly.py: assemble_stiffness (esparsa CSR) e assemble_stiffness_reduced. Molas de nó/elemento entram aqui.
  • Resolução — solver.py::solve particiona DOFs em free/fixed (_build_fixed_dofs, _augment_fixed_zero_stiffness), resolve o sistema reduzido e recupera reações como resíduo K·U − F nos DOFs fixos. Há caminhos paralelos que repetem esta lógica: _solve_geometric_nonlinear (P-Delta, ~l.1011), _solve_nonlinear_springs (~l.1230), _solve_modal (~l.1631) e _solve_spectrum (~l.1839). Qualquer mecanismo de constraint tem de ser aplicado de forma consistente nos cinco caminhos.
  • Modelo de dados — models.py: dataclasses Support, SupportAssignment, NodeSpring, etc. Coleções vivem em Structure2D.__init__ e há métodos add_* correspondentes.
  • Serialização — structure_io.py (_to_dict/carregamento), com espelho em SupportSet para variantes/faseamento; model_json.py para o formato .x2d legível/gerado por AI (com REQUIRED, missing_pieces, validação de referências).
  • Validação de topologia — model_check.py (nós isolados, coincidentes, duplicados, apoios atribuídos a nós inexistentes).
  • GUI — panels.py tem SupportPanel, NodeSpringPanel, ElemSpringPanel (tabelas BaseTablePanel); dialogs.py tem os diálogos correspondentes (SupportDialog, NodeSpringDialog, …). canvas.py desenha os apoios.
  • Assistente AI — as ferramentas expostas ao LLM (ai_context.py, tool_schema.py) são hoje só de leitura (consulta do modelo/resultados). A criação de modelo por AI é feita via JSON (model_json.py). A interação de edição do utilizador é pela GUI.

docs.title: 3. Decisão de motor: como impor a constraint no sistema
docs.text:
Três técnicas clássicas. Recomendação: transformação master–slave (redução de DOF) como método base, por ser exata, não introduzir DOFs extra e encaixar diretamente no particionamento free/fixed já existente.

Método Prós Contras Transformação (master–slave) U = T·U_m Exato; sem DOFs/parâmetros extra; K_r = Tᵀ K T, F_r = Tᵀ F; reações e pós-processamento limpos Requer eleger DOFs mestres e reescrever a assemblagem/recuperação; cadeias de constraints têm de ser resolvidas Multiplicadores de Lagrange Trata qualquer equação, inclusive redundantes; dá logo a "força de constraint" Aumenta o sistema (+1 DOF por equação); matriz deixa de ser definida positiva → afeta splu, modal (eigen) e P-Delta Penalização Trivial de somar a K (como uma mola muito rígida) Escolha do fator de penalização é frágil; mau condicionamento; constraint só aproximada

Proposta faseada:

  1. Fase 1 — implementar o método da penalização primeiro. É o de menor risco: um constraint Σ cᵢ·dofᵢ = g acrescenta α·cᵀc a K e α·g·c a F, somando na assemblagem exatamente como as molas já somam. Serve para validar toda a cadeia (dados → GUI → serialização → resultados) sem tocar no particionamento do solver. Escolher α relativo ao maior termo diagonal de K.
  2. Fase 2 — substituir/complementar pela transformação master–slave para ter constraints exatas e reações corretas, reutilizando o particionamento free/fixed. Só avançar depois de a Fase 1 estar validada por testes.

O documento assume esta ordem; a interface e a serialização são idênticas nas duas fases (só muda o interior do solver).

docs.title: 4. Modelo de dados (models.py + structure.py)
docs.text:
Nova dataclass, no espírito das existentes:

@dataclass
class Constraint:
    id: str
    kind: str            # 'equation' | 'equal_dof' | 'rigid_link'  (diafragma: versão futura)
    # forma canónica genérica: sum(coef_i * dof_i) = value
    terms: list          # list[(node_id, comp, coef)]  comp ∈ {'ux','uy','tz'}
    value: float = 0.0
    # campos de conveniência para os atalhos de alto nível:
    master: str = ""     # node_id mestre (rigid_link)
    slaves: list = None  # node_ids escravos
    components: list = None  # ex.: ['ux','tz'] para equal_dof
    enabled: bool = True
  • Coleção em Structure2D.__init__: self.constraints: dict[str, Constraint] = {}.
  • Métodos: add_constraint_equation(...), add_rigid_link(master, slaves, ...), add_equal_dof(nodes, components), remove_constraint(id). (add_diaphragm fica para versão futura.) Cada um invalida self._node_dof_index = None (à semelhança de add_node), porque a Fase 2 muda a contagem de DOFs livres.
  • Uma função expand_constraints(struc) -> list[equations] que converte os atalhos de alto nível na lista de equações canónicas (usando as coordenadas dos nós para o rigid link). Fica isolada e testável, no espírito de canonical_support_name.

docs.title: 5. Motor de resolução (assembly.py / solver.py)
docs.text:
Fase 1 (penalização):

  • Nova assembly._add_constraints(struc, K, F, alpha) chamada a seguir a _add_element_springs, somando α·cᵀc/α·g·c. alpha derivado de max(K.diagonal()).
  • Chamar em todos os pontos de montagem: solve, _solve_geometric_nonlinear, _solve_nonlinear_springs, _solve_modal (só a parte de K; não somar à massa), _solve_spectrum. Centralizar para evitar divergência (o próprio código já comenta o cuidado de "os dois caminhos nunca discordarem").

Fase 2 (transformação):

  • Construir T (esparsa, num_dofs × num_free_generalised) a partir das equações; DOFs escravos expressos em função dos mestres.
  • K_r = Tᵀ K T, F_r = Tᵀ F; resolver; recuperar U = T·U_m.
  • Reações e forças de constraint a partir do resíduo, como já se faz para apoios.
  • Detetar e rejeitar conflitos: escravo que também é apoio no mesmo DOF, cadeias circulares (A escravo de B, B escravo de A), mestre inexistente.

docs.title: 6. Serialização
docs.text:
• structure_io.py: acrescentar 'constraints': [...] em _to_dict e o carregamento simétrico. Não se acrescenta espelho em SupportSet: as constraints vivem só no modelo base e não participam em variantes/faseamento (decisão §9.3). Manter retro-compatibilidade: ficheiros antigos sem a chave carregam com constraints vazio.
  • model_json.py (.x2d): documentar constraints como coleção opcional (não entra em REQUIRED); acrescentar validação de referências em missing_pieces/mapa de referências (node_id das terms tem de existir); e um exemplo mínimo num dos templates. É aqui que o assistente AI passa a poder gerar constraints.

docs.title: 7. Validação (model_check.py)
docs.text:
Novas verificações, no estilo das existentes:

  • Term com node_id inexistente ou comp inválido.
  • Constraint que fixa um DOF já totalmente restringido por um apoio (redundância).
  • Nó escravo com apoio no mesmo componente (sobre-restrição/conflito).
  • Cadeias circulares / mestre que também é escravo.
  • Constraint sobre tz de nós que só têm elementos CST (esses nós não têm DOF rotacional ativo — coerente com a nota já existente sobre CST vs Allman).

docs.title: 8. Interface gráfica e interação com o utilizador
docs.text: Esta é a parte central do pedido. Três superfícies de interação, alinhadas com os padrões já usados no projeto.

docs.title: 8.1 Novo painel ConstraintPanel (panels.py)
docs.text: Uma tabela BaseTablePanel nova, irmã de SupportPanel/NodeSpringPanel, adicionada ao mesmo QTabWidget onde vivem apoios e molas. Colunas sugeridas: ID, Tipo, Mestre, Nós/Escravos, Componentes, Ativa. Botões adicionar/editar/remover como nos outros painéis.

docs.title: 8.2 Novo ConstraintDialog (dialogs.py)
docs.text:
Diálogo com o tipo no topo e campos que se adaptam ao tipo escolhido, para o utilizador nunca ter de escrever a equação à mão nos casos comuns:

  • Rigid link: escolher nó mestre + lista de escravos (multi-seleção).
  • Equal DOF: escolher nós + checkboxes ux/uy/tz.
  • Equação genérica (modo avançado): tabela de termos (nó, componente, coeficiente) + valor do lado direito.

Pré-visualização em texto da(s) equação(ões) resultante(s), reaproveitando expand_constraints, para o utilizador confirmar antes de gravar. Validação inline (reutilizar §7) com mensagem clara quando há conflito com um apoio.

docs.title: 8.3 Seleção no canvas (canvas.py)
docs.text: Fluxo "selecionar nós → botão direito → Criar constraint", pré-preenchendo o diálogo com os nós selecionados (o canvas já tem seleção de nós para apoios). Desenho das constraints: uma linha tracejada mestre↔escravos para rigid link/diafragma e um marcador distinto para equal-DOF, com uma entrada na legenda. Mostrar/ocultar via toggle de visualização.

docs.title: 8.4 Assistente AI (ai_context.py / tool_schema.py)
docs.text:
Duas frentes, sem sair do padrão atual (ferramentas de leitura + geração por JSON):

  1. Leitura — nova ferramenta de consulta get_constraints(struc, limit) no mesmo estilo de get_geometry/get_loads, e incluir uma linha-resumo em model_overview/summary_text ("N constraints: X rigid links, Y diafragmas"). Assim o assistente pode explicar as constraints de um modelo aberto.
  2. Criação — como a criação de modelo é feita por JSON .x2d, basta o §6 (documentar constraints em model_json.py, com exemplo e validação de missing_pieces) para o assistente passar a poder propor modelos com constraints. Mensagem de erro dedicada quando o utilizador define escravos mas esquece o mestre — o mesmo tipo de "par esquecido" que missing_pieces já apanha para supports/support_assignments.

docs.title: 8.5 Princípios de interação
docs.text:
• Nomes canónicos, não equações para o caso comum (rigid link, diafragma, equal DOF), reservando a equação genérica para um modo avançado — coerente com a filosofia CANONICAL_SUPPORTS do projeto ("um nome que tem de ser adivinhado é a falha que este projeto repete").
  • Feedback imediato: pré-visualização da equação e validação inline antes de gravar.
  • Consistência: o mesmo objeto Constraint alimenta GUI, .x2d, canvas e assistente — uma só fonte de verdade.

docs.title: 9. Decisões de âmbito (fixadas)
docs.text:
1. Método do solver: começar por penalização (Fase 1); master–slave (Fase 2) fica para depois de a Fase 1 estar validada por testes.
  2. Tipos na 1.ª versão: rigid link, equal DOF e equação genérica. O diafragma fica de fora desta versão (pode ser acrescentado depois como mais um atalho que gera equações, sem mudar o modelo de dados).
  3. Âmbito no modelo: constraints só no modelo base — não entram em variantes/faseamento nesta versão. Concretamente, não se acrescenta espelho em SupportSet (§6 fica sem essa parte).
  4. Assistente AI: ler e criar. Leitura via get_constraints + resumo; criação via .x2d (documentar/validar constraints em model_json.py, §6/§8.4).

docs.title: 10. Sequência de implementação sugerida
docs.text:
1. models.py + structure.py: dataclass Constraint, coleção, métodos add_*, expand_constraints, invalidação de node_dof_index.
  2. assembly.py/solver.py: _add_constraints por penalização nos cinco caminhos de solução.
  3. structure_io.py: guardar/carregar constraints.
  4. model_check.py: validações.
  5. panels.py + dialogs.py + canvas.py: painel, diálogo, seleção e desenho.
  6. model_json.py: documentar/validar constraints no .x2d.
  7. ai_context.py: get_constraints + resumo.
  8. Fase 2: transformação master–slave a substituir a penalização.
  9. Testes de verificação (tests/): rigid link vs. solução analítica; equal DOF; diafragma; carga/gravação round-trip do .x2d; consistência entre os cinco caminhos do solver; casos de conflito rejeitados por model_check. ```

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
xdfem2D includes member/section design to the Eurocodes, driven by the analysis results and the load combinations you choose:

  • Concrete — EN 1992-1-1 (EC2): reinforcement of rectangular bar sections and membrane (Wood/Baumann) reinforcement of concrete triangles, plus punching.
  • Steel — EN 1993-1-1 (EC3): cross-section resistance and member buckling of steel-section members.
  • Timber — EN 1995-1-1 (EC5): ULS member checks of timber-section members.

It is a design aid, not a substitute for engineering judgement: the concrete module covers rectangular sections in bending + shear, reports the required steel areas, and flags inadequate sections — it does not detail bars, check serviceability, or design columns for biaxial bending. See Licenses & Disclaimer for the full disclaimer that applies to every result the program produces, not just design.

Slabs and grillages

The bar design above applies to plane frames and grillage beams. For a plate slab, the Wood–Armer (W-A) design moments (m*x,bot, m*y,bot, m*x,top, m*y,top) are reported per triangle as results — the orthogonal-reinforcement moments an EC2 slab check consumes. See Slabs and Grillages.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before running a design, the model needs:

  1. Concrete sections — set the section's type to Concrete (Sections sub-tab). Only elements whose section is of type Concrete are designed.
  2. Material strengths — the section's material must carry a characteristic concrete strength fck and steel strength fyk (in its design properties). See supported classes below.
  3. A solved model — run the analysis first (F5); design uses the element force results.
  4. Combinations — design is performed for the load combinations (typically the ULS combinations); define them on the Combinations sub-tab or generate them with the automatic EN 1990 combinations.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
Everything lives in the Design menu (next to Analysis).

Step Menu What it does 1 Design → Code preferences Sets the code editions and partial factors — γc/γs/αcc (EC2), the γM factors (EC3/EC5), and the free-end buckling options. 2 Design → Design combinations Picks which combinations are checked (default: all available). 3 Design → Buckling lengths… Assigns the per-member buckling-length factors K for the steel/timber member checks. See Buckling lengths. 4 Design → Concrete/Steel/Timber… Runs the chosen design and fills the Design results table (or the coloured design view).

The Design menu items, after the two preferences entries and Buckling lengths…, are: Concrete Members (ULS), Concrete Members (SLS), Concrete Areas (ULS), Steel Members (ULS), Timber Members (ULS) and Punching….

Each concrete element is checked at its critical sections — both ends plus the span extremes of bending moment and shear — for every selected combination. The section requiring the most steel is marked as governing (★).

docs.title: Design codes
docs.text:
The default design code per material is set in File → Preferences → Design (concrete, steel, timber). The available options come from the same registry as Design → Code preferences — so concrete and timber offer their code editions (e.g. EN 1992-1-1:2004 / prEN 1992-1-1:2023, EN 1995-1-1:2004 / prEN 1995-1-1:2025) and steel offers EN 1993-1-1.

The code that a design run uses is recorded inside the .x2d. When you reopen a file that was already designed, its stored code takes precedence over the preference default, so a model keeps the code it was designed with. The active code is shown in the results header.

docs.title: Buckling lengths
docs.text:
The steel (EC3 §6.3.3) and timber (EC5) member checks need the buckling length of each physical member — a chain of collinear bars, identified automatically — not of each bar. The buckling length is L_cr = K × member length, per axis: K_y (major / in-plane), K_z (minor / out-of-plane) and K_LT (lateral torsional).

Open Design → Buckling lengths… to reveal the Buckling side panel:

  • The read-only table lists the members of the current canvas selection (expanded to whole physical members), with each bar's real length and the physical member length. Selecting a row highlights that member on the canvas.
  • Load from selection replaces the table with the current selection; Add from selection unions more members in; Load modified shows every member that already carries a K override.
  • Enter K_y / K_z / K_LT (use . as the decimal separator) and press Apply to selected or Apply to all — the values are written to every bar of the target members. Reset default clears the override (the member then follows the global default). OK closes the panel.

The model is 2D

Because the model is planar, xdfem2D cannot see the out-of-plane bracing. By default K_z uses the same member length as K_y (both default to 1.0), so the out-of-plane length equals the in-plane one unless you set K_z. Set the per-member K_z to reflect the real out-of-plane restraint.

docs.title: Free-end members (cantilevers)
docs.text:
When a physical member has a truly free end — a boundary node with nothing attached (no support, spring, other bar, triangle or constraint) — xdfem2D treats it as a cantilever and applies an automatic K to K_y and K_z (a free tip is unrestrained in both planes). K_LT is left on the global default. An explicit override you set always wins. Such members are flagged with a ⚑ in the Buckling table.

The behaviour is controlled in Design → Code preferences, group Buckling — free-end members (cantilevers): Auto K for a free (cantilever) end (on by default) and K for a free end (default 2.0; set e.g. 2.2 to allow for imperfect base fixity).

docs.title: Steel members (EC3)
docs.text: Design → Steel Members (ULS) runs the EN 1993-1-1 §6.2 (cross-section resistance: N, M_y, M_z, V, T) and §6.3.3 (member flexural + lateral torsional buckling) checks, once per physical member, over the selected combinations. Members need a section whose material is Steel and a supported shape (I, RHS/SHS, CHS). Results colour the Steel design view by utilisation and fill the Design table; the buckling lengths come from the K factors above.

docs.title: Timber members (EC5)
docs.text: Design → Timber Members (ULS) runs the EN 1995-1-1 ULS checks (N + M_y + M_z, V + T and the interactions, with the compression / LTB stability factors) once per physical member. The buckling lengths are obtained exactly like steel — same physical-member K factors. Results colour the Timber design view by ratio.

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
The Design results panel lists one row per critical section / combination:

Column Meaning Element, Combination, Location which member, combination and section Reason why the section was checked (end, M⁺/M⁻ peak, V peak) M_Ed, N_Ed, V_Ed design action effects at that section As,bot / As,top [cm²] required tension- and compression-face steel Asw/s [cm²/m] required shear reinforcement (stirrup area per metre) cot θ strut inclination used by the variable-angle truss Strut concrete strut crushing limit VRd,max Gov. ★ marks the governing section of each element

On the canvas you can also display the reinforcement envelopes along each member: the required longitudinal steel (As) view and the shear-reinforcement view show the maximum required steel along the span, enveloped over the selected design combinations.

docs.title: Design report
docs.text:
Design → Design report… opens a Design report side panel (a tab in the left dock, like the Punching and Buckling workbenches) that produces a full, step-by-step calculation report — every partial result, the code clause, the symbolic expression and the numeric substitution — for the checks the engine actually ran. The panel is read-only with respect to the model, so it can be used on a locked model.

Controls:

  • Material — lists only the design kinds present in the model: Steel members (EC3), Timber members (EC5), Concrete members (EC2) (bars / grillage), Concrete areas (EC2) (membrane / slab triangles) and Punching (EC2).
  • Scope — Whole model or Current selection (defaults to the current canvas selection). Selecting a row in the summary table highlights that member / element / column / triangle on the canvas.
  • Detail — Envelope (governing) gives one report per member (the governing case across the chosen combinations); Per combination gives one report per member and combination.
  • Combinations — a multi-select; nothing selected means all available.
  • Format — HTML (self-contained, with MathJax equations and a linked table of contents), PDF (composed pages with typeset equations and the section figure), Word (.docx, equations as images, or native editable OMML when pandoc is installed) and Markdown (with a sibling assets folder for the figures).

Preview renders the HTML and opens it; Export… saves in the chosen format. Each report embeds a small cross-section drawing (rectangle for concrete/timber, and the I / RHS / SHS / CHS outline for steel profiles).

docs.title: Report tools (pandoc / Ollama)
docs.text: Editable Word equations use pandoc, and the local AI assistant uses Ollama — both optional external tools. Preferences → Dependencies shows whether each is installed, explains what it unlocks, and offers the per-OS install command (copy or run). Without them the app still works: Word equations fall back to images, and the assistant uses the remote providers you configure.

docs.title: Method (EC2)
docs.text:
Flexure. Rectangular sections are designed for the dimensionless moment μ = M_Ed / (b·d²·fcd), giving the tension steel As; when μ exceeds the singly-reinforced limit, compression steel is added. The effective depth is d = h − cover. Minimum and maximum steel ratios follow EC2 §9.2.1.

Shear. The concrete resistance VRd,c (EC2 §6.2.2) is checked first. When the shear exceeds it, the variable-angle truss model (§6.2.3) is used: the strut angle is swept from cot θ = 2.5 (θ ≈ 21.8°) down to cot θ = 1.0 (θ = 45°), choosing the flattest strut the concrete can carry so the stirrup demand Asw/s is minimised, while respecting the strut-crushing limit VRd,max. If the section crushes even at θ = 45°, it is reported as inadequate in shear at the crushing limit. The truss and VRd,c formulas are delegated to eurocodepy.

All partial safety factors come from the Code-preferences dialog: fcd = αcc·fck/γc and fyd = fyk/γs.

docs.title: Material strengths
docs.text:
Strengths are looked up from the standard class strings:

  • Concrete fck [MPa]: C12/15, C16/20, C20/25, C25/30, C30/37, C35/45, C40/50, C45/55, C50/60 (a bare C30 form is also accepted).
  • Steel fyk [MPa]: A400 / A500 (and the B/S400, B/S500 variants).

docs.title: SAP2000 interchange
docs.text: When you export to SAP2000, concrete materials are written as Eurocode 2-2004 design data (concrete strength, a rebar material, per-frame design procedure, section cover and the EC2 preferences), and the load combinations are marked for concrete design. Importing a .s2k reads this back. See Exporting → SAP2000.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Rectangular sections only; flexure about the in-plane axis plus shear.
  • ULS reinforcement only — no SLS (crack/deflection) checks and no bar detailing.
  • Columns are not designed for axial + biaxial bending interaction.

docs.title: Domains (plane vs plate)
docs.text:
Every xdfem2D model lives in one of two domains. The choice is made once, in New model, and is fixed for the model's life — because every support, load and result changes meaning between them, there is no switching.

Domain What it is Elements DOFs per node Typical use Plane a frame or wall in its own plane frame bars, membrane triangles (CST / Allman / ES-FEM) ux, uy, θz frames, trusses, walls Plate a slab or grillage bending out of plane grillage beams, plate-bending triangles (MITC3 / DKT) w, θx, θy slabs, beam grillages

Both domains carry three degrees of freedom per node — the solver machinery is shared — but the three slots mean different things, so the same storage reads as ux, uy, θz in a plane model and w, θx, θy in a plate one.

docs.title: Choosing the domain
docs.text: New model shows the two domains as clickable icon cards — a portal frame with a shear wall for Frame / Wall (in-plane), and a supported slab field for Slab / Grillage (out-of-plane). Click a card to select it (the border highlights); a double-click selects and confirms in one gesture. A coloured domain badge in the toolbar (blue Plane / green Plate) then shows which one is active, and the window title carries the document name.

docs.title: What follows from the domain
docs.text:
The interface is domain-aware throughout — the same primitives read correctly in either domain (see Topology):

Aspect Plane Plate Line element role Beam Grid member Area element role Panel (membrane) Slab (MITC3 / DKT) Supports PIN, FIXED, ROLLER-X/Y, GUIDED-X/Y, BLOCK SIMPLE, CLAMPED, CLAMP-X/Y, SYM-X/Y, BLOCK Loads Fx, Fy, Mz; edge tractions Fz, Mx, My; area pressure pz; Winkler kz Triangle results membrane stresses σ (with an N=σ·t force toggle) slab forces: moments, shears, Wood–Armer Dynamics in-plane modes; P-Delta available vertical (out-of-plane) modes; no P-Delta

Each topic page covers both domains: Modelling, Loads, Analysis, Results and Design. For a plate-focused orientation and worked scripts, see Slabs and Grillages.

docs.title: Engine Reference
docs.text:
The calculation engine (xdfem2d) is usable on its own, without the interface. This page documents what it exposes: the Python API (a) and the JSON data structure (b) that .x2d/.json files store.

Units are metres, kN, kN·m and kN/m². Angles are in degrees where an angle is named. A model has a fixed domain — plane (frames/walls: ux, uy, θz) or plate (slabs/grillages: w, θx, θy); the three DOF slots keep the same positions in both, only their meaning changes.

from xdfem2d import Structure2D
s = Structure2D(domain="plane")   # or "plate"

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
Everything below is a method of Structure2D, except "Section cuts", "Member buckling" and "Design reports", which live as plain functions in their own Qt-free modules (xdfem2d.cuts, xdfem2d.steel_members, xdfem2d.design_report) — each of those sections says so again where it starts. Signatures omit self; … -> Type is the object returned. Loads take a positive value in the axis direction (gravity is negative). In the plate domain the aliases fz/mx/my, w/tx/ty, kz/ktx/kty fill the same slots as fx/fy/mz, ux/uy/tz, kx/ky/kt.

The sections below follow the order in which a model is typically built: model + solve, materials/sections, elements, geometry, supports, loads, analysis, constraints — then the simplified facade and the design layer (buckling, reports).

The create_* / add_* convention, used throughout this document: most things can be built two ways — a create_* shortcut (a magnitude/name, sane defaults, get-or-create where that makes sense; prefer this) or the generic add_* call it forwards to (every field spelled out; reach for it only when a shortcut cannot express what you need — a local-frame load with both components, a trapezoidal axial load, and similar). Each subsection below lists the create_* layer directly above the add_* layer it delegates to, so the two stay next to each other instead of the convention being re-explained per subsection.

A few terms are used interchangeably below for the same thing: "geometry object", "surface object" and "region" all mean an item in geometry_objects (a GeoRectangle, GeoPolygon, GeoSegment, …, meshed into bars/triangles/quads at solve time) — the canonical name in code and in the JSON structure is geometry object.

docs.title: Model, solve and I/O
docs.text:
Structure2D(domain="plane")
calculate() -> dict                         # assemble + solve; returns results
check_references()                          # raise on dangling/invalid refs
domain_problems() -> list[str]              # features unsupported by the domain
save(path)                                  # write .x2d / .json
load(path) -> Structure2D                   # (classmethod-style) read a file

docs.title: Materials and sections
docs.text: create_* (convenience) directly above the add_* (fundamental) it forwards to — see the convention note above.

docs.title: Materials — create_* (convenience)
docs.text:
create_material(...)                                    # == add_material, pure alias
create_rc_material(concrete="C30/37", steel="B500B",
                   name=None) -> Material                # get-or-create, deduped by name
create_steel_material(steel="S275", name=None) -> Material
create_timber_material(timber="C24", name=None) -> Material

name=None derives the name from the class string (e.g. "C30/37"). Get-or-create: two calls with the same class dedupe to one Material.

docs.title: Materials — add_* (fundamental)
docs.text:
add_material(name, elastic_modulus, unit_weight, alpha=1e-5, unit_mass=None,
             material_type=None, design=None, poisson=0.2) -> Material
add_concrete_material(material_name, concrete_class, steel_class,
                      gamma_c=1.5, gamma_s=1.15, alpha_cc=1.0) -> ConcreteMaterial

add_concrete_material links EC2 design metadata onto an already-existing material by name — a different job from create_rc_material, which makes the physical material itself.

docs.title: Sections — create_* (convenience)

docs.title: Supports — convenience
docs.text:
pin(nodes)                   # plane: ux,uy   · plate: w
fix(nodes)                   # plane: ux,uy,θz · plate: w,θx,θy
roller(nodes, free="x")      # plane only — frees one translation
symm(nodes, axis="x")        # plate only — symmetry line (w free, θ about axis fixed)
create_support(nodes, ux=False, uy=False, tz=False, w=None, tx=None, ty=None,
               name=None)

nodes: a single id/Node, or a list of either (same list-or-single rule as loads). pin/fix/roller/symm cover the common cases with an auto-assigned canonical support name ("PIN", "FIXED", "ROLLER-X", "SYM-X", …); create_support is the generic one-call create-and-assign underneath them.

True fixes that DOF, False frees it — every flag defaults to False, so create_support(nodes) on its own restrains nothing. A model that means to fully fix a node has to say ux=True, uy=True, tz=True (or just call fix(nodes)); writing all three explicitly as False "to be clear" restrains nothing and turns the structure into a mechanism — a real mistake a script has made. w/tx/ty are the plate-domain aliases of the same three (ux,uy,tz) slots.

docs.text:
add_support(name, ux=False, uy=False, tz=False, w=None, tx=None, ty=None) -> Support
assign_support(node_id, support_name) -> SupportAssignment

The two calls every convenience wrapper above forwards to: create the named restraint, then assign it to a node. Reach for these directly to reuse one named Support across many assign_support calls without re-specifying its flags each time.

docs.title: Supports on an edge — support_edge (and pin_edge / fix_edge / …)
docs.text:
support_edge(object_id, edge, kind="pin")            # the general call
pin_edge(object_id, edge)                 # = support_edge(…, 'pin')   plate SIMPLE · plane PIN
fix_edge(object_id, edge)                 # = support_edge(…, 'fix')   plate CLAMPED · plane FIXED
roller_edge(object_id, edge, free="x")    # = support_edge(…, 'roller-x'/'roller-y')  plane only
symm_edge(object_id, edge, axis="x")      # = support_edge(…, 'symm-x'/'symm-y')      plate only
support_object_edge(object_id, edge, support_name)    # any named support / 'free'
free_edge(object_id, edge)                            # remove — clear that edge

support_edge is the general call; pin_edge/fix_edge/roller_edge/ symm_edge are it with a fixed kind. edge: 'all' | 'bottom'/'right'/'top'/'left' | an integer index (vertex i → i+1, wrapping) — the same vocabulary create_edge_load (see "### Loads") uses. kind: pin | fix | symm-x | symm-y | roller-x | roller-y. All are domain-aware (roller-* is plane-only, symm-* plate-only, exactly as the node methods are) and resolve to the canonical support (SIMPLE/CLAMPED/…).

They all write the object's per-edge edge_supports list, so every mesh node the edge generates is restrained, and restraints can differ per edge (e.g. clamped / simply / clamped / simply around a rectangle). This is the reliable route: an earlier support_edge restrained only the two corner nodes and left edge_support_mode to propagate the rest — the approach the per-edge list was added to replace.

support_object_edge takes an explicit support name instead of a kind: any support already defined (or a canonical name such as SIMPLE / CLAMPED), or 'free' to clear that edge. free_edge is the inverse of the whole family — it frees an edge whether it was restrained through the edge_supports list or by corner-node assignments.

In a JSON model the same thing is the object's "edge_supports" key: a list with one entry per edge in perimeter order (a rectangle is bottom, right, top, left), each a support name or "free". For example, a slab simply supported on two opposite edges:

{ "kind": "rectangle", "id": "R1", "tri_section_name": "Slab",
  "node_ids": ["R1.p0", "R1.p1", "R1.p2", "R1.p3"],
  "edge_supports": ["SIMPLE", "free", "SIMPLE", "free"] }

When edge_supports is absent, edge_support_mode ("common" default / "equal" / "none") instead propagates each edge from whatever supports its two corner nodes carry — the older corner-propagation fallback, used when the corners are supported directly (assign_support/pin on the corner nodes) rather than through edge_supports.

docs.title: Bar and area loads — create_* (convenience)
docs.text:
create_bar_uniform_load(elements, load_case_id=None, q=None, direction="down")     # UDL on a bar or geo line object
create_bar_distributed_load(elements, load_case_id=None, q_i=None, q_j=None, direction="down")  # trapezoidal; bars only
create_bar_point_load(elements, load_case_id=None, p=None, at=0.5, direction="down")  # bars only; at = span fraction
create_area_uniform_load(targets, load_case_id=None, p=None, direction="down")  # slab (plate); area equivalent of the above

elements/targets: a single id/object, or a list of either (list in, list out). load_case_id optional: omitted/None uses a default case ("LC1"), auto-created on first use. direction: "down" (gravity: −Y plane / −Z plate), "up", "perp" (⊥ to the bar, local) and "axial" — the last two bars only, plane domain (create_bar_distributed_load only takes "down"/"up"). On a geometry line id (GeoSegment/GeoMultisegment/ GeoArc), create_bar_uniform_load forwards to add_line_distributed_load instead ("down"/"up" only — no local axis before meshing).

create_area_uniform_load is the area/region counterpart of the three bar shortcuts above — the same "one value, spread uniformly" idea, applied to a geometry object (every triangle/quad it meshes into) or a single tri/quad element instead of a bar. Plate domain only; targets accepts an id, object, or list.

It carries "uniform" in its name even though the physical quantity is a pressure [kN/m²], not a line load [kN/m] — that's a naming choice, not a unit mismatch. The reason: api_reference_tool's name lookup matches on substrings of the method name, not on the docstring. An assistant whose add_uniform_load call failed (wrong target — that's the bar method) and who then searches for "uniform" needs the area facade to turn up by that same word, not only by "area" or "pressure".

create_node_load(nodes, load_case_id=None, p=None, direction="down") -> PointLoad

The load/temperature removes take a load_case_id="" that clears every case on the target, or one named case.

docs.title: Removal facade — delete_* / free_edge
docs.text:
The intent-level inverses of the create_*/pin/support layer — the removal twin of create_*, and what to reach for when undoing an edit:

delete_support(nodes)                 # unassign the support on a node / list of nodes
free_edge(object_id, edge)            # free an edge (inverse of support_edge/pin_edge)
delete_area(object_id)                # delete a region/line object (= remove_geo_object)
delete_load(target, load_case_id="")  # node / bar / area loads on a target
delete_temperature(target, load_case_id="")   # bar / triangle / quad / object
delete_spring(target)                 # node / element / area / line spring

Each is a forgiving wrapper over the low-level remove_*: removing what is not there is a no-op, so one delete_load('N1') clears whatever loads N1 carries without the caller first classifying the target. The low-level remove_* are the by-id/by-name primitives (used by the GUI and scripts); the delete_*/ free_edge facade is the one the assistant browses and uses.

Advanced entry points (variants, construction sequences, support sets, with_active, derive_variant, stiffness_hash) support the staging and study features and are documented with those.

add_cut(id, x1, y1, x2, y2, name="") -> Cut
remove_cut(cut_id)
rename_cut(old_id, new_id)

A Cut is a straight segment (x1,y1) -> (x2,y2) that reports the resultant of the internal forces crossing it — bars and areas, combined and separately — for one case (load case, analysis case, or SomaLinear combination) at a time. Evaluation lives in the Qt-free xdfem2d.cuts module, not on Structure2D itself:

cut_result(struc, results, cut, case, ref_point=None) -> dict
    # {'domain', 'bars': [...], 'areas': [...],
    #  'resultant': {'bars', 'areas', 'total'}, 'reason'}
    # bars/areas per-crossing detail; resultant['total'] is what a Results
    # panel shows. ref_point defaults to the cut's own midpoint.
cut_distribution(cutres, n=101) -> dict
    # {'s', 'fields', 'markers'} — sampled per-length area fields (piecewise
    # constant per triangle) plus bar crossings as point markers, for
    # plotting the distribution along the cut.
cuts_report(struc, results, cases, ref_point=None) -> list[dict]
    # one row per (cut, case): cut_id, cut_name, case, total_<N|V|M or
    # V|Mb|Mt>, reason — every cut against every case id, for CSV export.

cut_bar_resultant(struc, results, cut, case, ref_point=None) -> dict
cut_area_resultant(struc, results, cut, case, ref_point=None) -> dict
    # the two halves cut_result sums; called directly only if you want one
    # side in isolation.
find_bar_crossings(struc, cut) -> list[dict]        # {elem_id, a, s, x, y}
find_triangle_crossings(struc, cut) -> list[dict]    # {tri_id, s0, s1, p0, p1}
    # pure geometry — every bar/triangle the cut crosses, no results needed.

Resultant keys are N, V, M for a plane cut (axial along the cut's normal, shear along its tangent, in-plane moment about ref_point) or V, Mb, Mt for a plate cut (transverse shear, bending and twisting moment — the same mn/mnt split slab results already use). struc must be the compiled model (geo_expand.expand_geometry's output) when the model has geometry objects, matching whatever handle the GUI already keeps for tri-field plotting — cuts are evaluated against the solved mesh, not the editable objects. See dev/CUT_PLAN.md for the sign conventions, the tolerance policy at element edges/nodes, and the phase-by-phase implementation notes.

docs.title: Simplified API (the "simple" facade)
docs.text:
Thin, lossless shortcuts over the generic methods for the common cases: a magnitude + a named direction instead of signed components and a reference frame, and a support created and assigned in one call. They read the model's domain and adapt (plane vs plate), and raise a clear error when a direction or support does not apply. Nothing new is stored — each forwards to the generic method, so a model built this way is identical to the long form.

Not a separate block of its own: every create_* shortcut is documented next to the add_* call it forwards to, under that call's own domain heading above — loads, supports, materials/sections/nodes/geometry, and load/analysis cases each pair create_* (convenience) with add_* (fundamental) in one place, instead of repeating either here.

docs.title: Compatibility appendix
docs.text:
Every name below still works exactly as documented historically — nothing was removed or renamed away, only given a canonical counterpart. The JSON file format does not change: whichever name builds the model, save() writes the same thing.

Still works (unchanged) Canonical name Notes add_rc_section create_rc_section same signature, pure rename add_steel_section create_steel_section same signature, pure rename add_panel create_area same signature, pure rename add_geo_line add_geo_segment pure rename, both still work add_geo_polyline add_geo_multisegment pure rename, both still work add_geo_surface add_geo_polygon pure rename, both still work

No name in this table is deprecated or warns — every one is a permanent alias. add_concrete_material, add_material, add_section, add_tri_section, add_quad_section, add_plate_section, add_node, add_bar_element, add_tri_element, add_quad_element, pin/fix/roller/symm, add_support_settlement, and every generic add_* load/support/analysis call keep their original names unchanged — they are the fundamental layer the create_* convenience methods forward to, not aliases themselves. add_area_section/add_area_element are a newer addition to that same fundamental layer, not a replacement for add_tri_*/add_quad_*: they pair/dispatch to them for a caller that does not know tri vs quad up front, while every existing tri/quad call site keeps calling the single-shape methods directly. See dev/XDFEM2D_ENGINE.md for the full design rationale and phased implementation history.

Exception — the pre-existing simple-facade load calls do not follow this rule. add_bar_load, add_bar_point_load, add_node_load, add_pressure, add_self_weight and add_temperature are gone, with no alias: renamed outright to create_bar_uniform_load, create_bar_point_load, create_node_load, create_area_uniform_load, create_self_weight and create_temperature. Unlike everything else in this document, this is a real, unqualified rename — the project had not shipped when it was made, so there was no installed base calling the old names to protect.

create_area_uniform_load itself went through two further renames after that, both for the same reason (findability by an assistant searching api_reference_tool, whose name argument matches a substring of the method name, not the docstring):

  1. From create_pressure — "pressure" had no lexical link back to a bar's distributed/uniform load, so an assistant asked for a distributed load on a slab region had no way to find it by name.
  2. From create_area_load — the resulting name still had no lexical link to "uniform", so an assistant whose add_uniform_load call failed (the fundamental bar method — wrong for an area target) and who searched for "uniform" next still found no area-load facade.

See dev/XDFEM2D_ENGINE.md for the full reasoning.

docs.title: Member buckling (steel EC3 / timber EC5)
docs.text:
The steel and timber member checks work on physical members — chains of collinear bars grouped by xdfem2d.steel_members.identify_members(struc). Each BarElement carries the per-member buckling-length factors used by the design (buckling length = K × physical-member length); leave them None to inherit the global default from the design preferences:

BarElement.sd_ky   # K for flexural buckling about y (major / in-plane)
BarElement.sd_kz   # K for flexural buckling about z (minor / out-of-plane)
BarElement.sd_klt  # K for the lateral-torsional length
BarElement.sd_ltb  # bool: member susceptible to lateral-torsional buckling

Free-end (cantilever) detection helpers in xdfem2d.steel_members:

member_free_ends(struc, member)   -> (free_i, free_j)   # a truly-free end node
member_has_free_end(struc, member) -> bool
cantilever_k_for(struc, member, prefs) -> float | None  # auto K (Ky, Kz) or None

A node is a free end when nothing is attached to it (a single incident bar and no support, node spring, triangle or constraint). When enabled (cantilever_auto, default on), such members take cantilever_k (default 2.0) for sd_ky/sd_kz unless an explicit value is set.

docs.title: Design reports (calculation trace)
docs.text:
Every design routine can, with with_reports=True, attach a full step-by-step calculation report for the governing case of each member / section / column / triangle. The report content — clause, symbolic expression, LaTeX and numeric substitution — is produced by eurocodepy through an optional trace (eurocodepy.calc_report.CalcReport): the check computes exactly as before and the trace only records what was computed, so the reported numbers are, by construction, the ones used. The app only gathers and renders; it never re-derives formulas.

The EC2 procedures are owned by eurocodepy composites, each taking an input dataclass and an optional trace:

eurocode2_shear_check(ShearInput, v_ed, trace=None)      # §6.2 shear
eurocode2_punching_check(PunchInput, n_ed, …, trace=None) # §6.4 / :2023 §8.4
eurocode2_membrane_check(MembraneInput, trace=None)       # §6.109 membrane (areas)
eurocode2_slab_check(SlabInput, trace=None)               # §6.1 slab flexure (areas)
calc_torsion(…, trace=None)                               # §6.3 grillage torsion
calc_asl_nm(…, trace=None)                                # §6.1 M-N flexure

Gathering and rendering live in xdfem2d.design_report (Qt-free):

build_reports(struc, results, material, prefs=None, combinations=None) -> {id: report}
    # material: "steel" | "timber" | "concrete" | "concrete_area" | "punching"
filter_reports(reports, material, struc,
               selected_bars=None, selected_nodes=None, selected_tris=None)
reports_from(design_output) -> {id: report}      # normalise a routine's output
report_base_id(report) -> str                    # member/element/column/triangle id
per_combination_key(base_id, combo) / merge_per_combination({combo: {id: report}})
render_html(reports, title)   / render_markdown(...) / render_pdf(...) / render_docx(...)
write_markdown_bundle(reports, md_path, title)   # .md + <stem>_assets/ figures
section_figure_png(geom)      # cross-section drawing (rect / I / RHS / SHS / CHS)
pandoc_available()            # gates the native editable-OMML Word route
EXPECTED_SCHEMA / schema_mismatches(reports)     # report-schema version guard

A report dict has the shape {schema_version, title, meta, sections:[{title, steps:[{symbol, value, unit, clause, expr, latex, subst, note, ok}]}]}. The GUI consumes these through the Design → Design report… side panel.

docs.title: Notes on the slots
docs.text:
• The three per-node components are positional: they are written with the canonical (plane) names ux/uy/tz, fx/fy/mz, kx/ky/kt in both domains. In a plate model read them as w/θx/θy, fz/mx/my, kz/kθx/kθy. Readers also accept the plate aliases on input.
  • geometry_objects[].kind is one of segment, arc, multisegment, rectangle, polygon. The old spellings line, polyline, surface are still read. Line-like objects carry section_name, divisions, max_chord; area-like objects carry tri_section_name, target_size, edge_support_mode, edge_spring_mode.
  • tri_sections[].formulation is CST, Allman or ES-FEM (panel / membrane) in the plane domain, or a plate-bending element in the plate domain: MITC3 (shear-deformable, the default — valid for thin and thick slabs) or DKT (thin-plate / Kirchhoff).
