docs.title: Exporting
docs.text: Import and export live in the File menu — Import… brings a model in from another tool, Export… writes the model out to a CAD/analysis format, and the report/table/drawing commands below produce deliverables.

docs.title: Drawing
docs.text: File → Print Graphics… (Ctrl+E) saves the current canvas as PNG, SVG, or PDF, with options for resolution (PNG), transparency, tight bounding box, and grid visibility.

docs.title: Report — Write Report…
docs.text:
File → Write Report… (Ctrl+Shift+W) is the main report command. A single dialog lets you choose the format and the content:

  • Format — PDF (paginated A4, each case/combination on a new page, with title, timestamp and page number), Word (.docx, editable — needs python-docx), or Excel (.xlsx — needs openpyxl).
  • Content — any mix of: project info; the structure and loads drawings; the model tables; the result tables; the result views (deformed, diagrams, stress, …) for the cases you tick; and the design views. Result content requires a solved model.

docs.title: Tables to Excel — Write Tables to Excel…
docs.text:
File → Write Tables to Excel… (Ctrl+Shift+T) is the one-click shortcut: the model tables — plus the result tables if the model has been solved — go straight into a single .xlsx workbook, with no dialog. Headers are bold with frozen panes and auto-fit columns; sheets with no data are omitted.

Model sheets:

Sheet Contents Materials E, γ, α, unit mass Sections material, b, h, area, inertia Nodes ID, X, Y Elements ID, node i/j, section, hinges Supports node, support, UX/UY/TZ Node / Element springs stiffnesses Load cases ID, action type, self-weight factor Point / Distributed / Temperature loads, Settlements, Nodal masses per load case Analysis cases ID, type, coefficients, modal/spectrum/stored-K Combinations ID, type, analysis-case coefficients Spectral functions ID, description, damping, (T, Sa) points

Result sheets (when solved):

Sheet Columns Displacements Case type, Case, Node, ux, uy, rz Reactions Case type, Case, Node, Rx, Ry, Mz (with a bold Σ row per case) Constraint forces Case type, Case, Node, Fx, Fy, Mz (only if the model has constraints) Element forces Case type, Case, Element, End (i/j), N, V, M Span extremes Case, Element, |N|max, |V|max, M⁺, M⁻ Reaction sums Case type, Case, ΣRx, ΣRy, ΣMz Modal Case, Mode, ω, f, T, Meff_X%, Meff_Y%, Cum X%, Cum Y%

docs.title: CAD and other tools
docs.text:
File → Export… writes the model to one of several interchange formats; the chosen file filter drives the target:

Format Extension Direction SAP2000 text .s2k export and import DXF drawing .dxf export and import IFC (openBIM) .ifc export and import Autodesk Robot text .str export Python build script .py export — includes variants, support sets, variant combinations, and construction sequences

DXF exports the geometry as a drawing and imports a drawing back into a model (lines become bars); it is the bridge to general CAD. Robot export writes the Autodesk Robot Structural Analysis text format. The Python export writes a script that rebuilds the model with the xdfem2d API — handy for versioning or programmatic edits — including variants, support sets, variant combinations, and construction sequences with all their phases and operations. Import… reads SAP2000 .s2k, DXF, or IFC.

docs.title: SAP2000 (.s2k)
docs.text:
xdfem2D can export to and import from the SAP2000 text interchange format (.s2k). The 2-D model is mapped to a planar SAP model in the X–Z plane (xdfem2D X → SAP X, xdfem2D Y → SAP Z), with the out-of-plane DOFs deactivated. This is a best-effort exchange — open the file in SAP2000 and verify a simple case (especially moment/temperature sign conventions).

What is exchanged:

xdfem2D SAP2000 Load case Load pattern (SAP auto-creates its Linear Static case) Linear analysis case Linear Static case NonLinear analysis case (unilateral springs) Nonlinear Static case (no P-Delta) Geometric Nonlinear (P-Delta) Nonlinear Static case (P-Delta) Modal / Spectrum / Mass Modal / Response-Spectrum case + Mass Source Combination (SomaLinear) Linear-Add combination Node spring Joint spring (uncoupled, bilateral only) Element (Winkler) spring Frame line spring; tension-/compression-only mode maps to the SAP "SimpleType" Concrete materials EC2 (Eurocode 2-2004) design data: concrete strength, rebar material, per-frame design procedure, section cover, and design preferences (γc, γs, αcc)

Unilateral node springs

SAP joint springs are linear/bilateral, so a node spring's tension-/compression-only mode is not exported. Use a compression-/tension-only element spring (or a nonlinear link in SAP) to model unilateral support along a member. Element-spring modes round-trip both ways.

Concrete design under Eurocode 2

When the model carries concrete materials, the export sets the concrete frame design code to Eurocode 2-2004 and marks the load combinations for concrete design, so SAP runs the RC design under EC2. Importing a .s2k reads the concrete strength, safety factors and per-frame design flag back into xdfem2D.

docs.title: IFC (.ifc)
docs.text:
xdfem2D can export to and import from IFC — the openBIM ISO 16739 exchange format — using the structural-analysis view (IfcStructuralAnalysisModel). This is the branch of IFC meant for finite-element exchange, so it mirrors the xdfem2D model closely; it is not the physical/architectural model (IfcBeam, IfcSlab, …). IFC support needs the optional ifcopenshell package — install the engine with the ifc extra (pip install "xdfem2d[ifc]"); the desktop app already includes it.

Values use the same unit convention SAP2000 itself writes — kN, m, tonne, °C (force in kilonewtons, mass in tonnes, temperature in degrees Celsius) — with every unit, including the derived ones for elastic modulus, mass density, thermal expansion and line/area force, declared in the file so importers resolve the material and load units without warnings. Only nodes attached to a member are written (an isolated node is not a valid structural point connection).

The 2-D model is placed in 3-D space by domain, following the SAP2000 convention: a plane model lies in the global X–Z plane (Y = 0) and a plate model in the X–Y plane (Z = 0). On import the plane is detected from the geometry and the domain inferred (X–Z → plane, X–Y → plate).

What is exchanged:

xdfem2D IFC (structural analysis) Model IfcStructuralAnalysisModel Node IfcStructuralPointConnection Bar element IfcStructuralCurveMember (+ IfcProfileDef for the section) Triangle / quad IfcStructuralSurfaceMember (thickness carried) Material IfcMaterial + Pset_MaterialMechanical (E, ν, density) Support IfcBoundaryNodeCondition on the point connection Load case IfcStructuralLoadCase Nodal load IfcStructuralPointAction Bar distributed load IfcStructuralLinearAction Area (slab) pressure IfcStructuralPlanarAction

Domain choice on import

If the geometry does not identify a plane (for example a single line of nodes), the importer asks whether to read the file as a plane or a plate model, just like the SAP2000 import. A genuinely three-dimensional IFC model (nodes varying out of a single plane) cannot be imported as a 2-D model and is reported rather than silently flattened.

Best-effort exchange

A trapezoidal bar load is exported at its mean intensity, and the FE mesh of a slab is exchanged as its surface members (re-meshed on import). Open the file in an IFC viewer and verify a simple case before relying on it.

Physical-model files

Many BIM tools export only the physical model (IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcSlab, …) with no structural-analysis model. When you import such a file, xdfem2D offers to bring in the geometry only — beam/column centre-lines as drawing polylines and slab/wall outlines as polygon regions — with no supports, loads, materials or sections. It is a drafting aid to trace over, not an analysis import.

docs.title: .x2d — native format (recommended)
docs.text:
A .x2d file is a ZIP archive containing:

Entry Contents structure.json the full model (nodes, elements, materials, sections, supports, springs, constraints, loads, load cases, analysis cases, combinations, spectral functions, nodal masses) results.json analysis results, when present — including any reinforcement / steel / timber design payloads and the design code they were produced with (which takes precedence over the preference default on reopen) stiffness_<id>.npy stored tangent stiffness matrices from P-Delta runs view.json display options, selection, and Scenes (with per-scene zoom)

This is the default for Save / Open and preserves everything, including the view state.

docs.title: .json — structure only
docs.text: A plain JSON export of the model (no results, no view state). Useful for interchange and version control.

docs.title: Migration of combinations
docs.text: When an older model that stored load-case factors directly in combinations is opened, xdfem2D folds each such factor into a Linear analysis case and rewrites the combination to reference that analysis case. This keeps the three-tier model consistent and is applied automatically on load and before solving.

docs.title: Units
docs.text: All files use the program's units throughout: kN · m · kNm (and t for mass).

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This walkthrough builds, solves, and reviews a simple frame in a few minutes.

docs.title: 1. Start from a template
docs.text:
Choose File → New from Template… (Ctrl+T). The first option is Portal Frame. Set the span and height, review the material/section defaults, and click OK. The structure is drawn and automatically fitted to the canvas.

Every template comes with:

  • a self-weight load case LC1 (self-weight multiplier = 1.0), and
  • a Linear analysis case SW that applies LC1.

See Templates for the full list.

docs.title: 2. Add loads (optional)
docs.text: Open the Loads tab in the left panel to add point loads, distributed loads, thermal loads, or settlements. Each load belongs to a load case. See Loads.

docs.title: 3. Define analysis cases and combinations
docs.text:
• An analysis case says how to solve (Linear, Modal, Spectrum, …) and which load cases to apply with what factors.
  • A combination combines analysis cases (e.g. ULS = 1.35·G + 1.5·Q).

Adding a load case automatically creates a matching Linear analysis case, so for simple models you may not need to define any analysis cases by hand. See Analysis.

docs.title: 4. Run the analysis
docs.text: Press F5 (or the Run button in the toolbar). When results are available the model is locked (the padlock shows closed); unlock with Ctrl+L to edit again.

docs.title: 5. Review results
docs.text: Use the View dropdown in the toolbar (or View → View mode, Ctrl+1…Ctrl+8) to switch between Structure, Loads, Deformed shape, Bending moment, Shear force, Axial force, Reactions, and Modal shapes. Pick the Case to display. The Results tab shows the full numeric report. See Results.

docs.title: 6. Save and export
docs.text:
• File → Save (Ctrl+S) writes a .x2d file (structure + results + view).
  • File → Write Report… produces a PDF/Word/Excel report; Write Tables to Excel… is the one-click spreadsheet.

See Exporting and File Formats.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: xdfem2D targets Python 3.12+ and uses uv for dependency management.

docs.title: Runtime dependencies
docs.text:
• matplotlib — canvas rendering and PDF export
  • numpy — analysis core
  • pyside6 — desktop interface
  • openpyxl — Excel results export
  • eurocodepy — Eurocode helpers (RC design, EC0 combinations)

docs.title: Install with uv
docs.text:
# from the project root
uv sync

This creates a virtual environment and installs everything in pyproject.toml.

docs.title: Run the application
docs.text:
uv run xdfem2d
# or
uv run python -m xdfem2d.xdfem2d_gui

docs.title: Building the documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is written for MkDocs with the Material theme.

# install the docs toolchain (one-off)
uv pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material

# live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
uv run mkdocs serve

# build a static site into ./site
uv run mkdocs build

Once built, the in-app Help → Documentation (or F1) opens the local site/index.html.

docs.title: The Interface
docs.text: The main window has three regions: a menu bar and tool bar across the top, the left tabs for model input and results, and the canvas on the right.

docs.title: Tool bar
docs.text:
The tool bar groups appear in a fixed order. The first three are always visible:

Group Contents File New, Open, Save, Run analysis, Lock/Unlock Zoom Zoom window, zoom in, zoom out, fit View / Case View-mode dropdown, Case dropdown, mode/scale controls

The remaining groups — Scene, Add, Edit/Delete — can be shown or hidden from View → Tool bar: … or in Preferences.

docs.title: Menus
docs.text:
• File — New, New from Template, Open (+ Recent), Import… (SAP2000 .s2k, DXF), Save / Save As, Export… (SAP2000 .s2k, DXF, Robot .str, Python script), Write Report… (Word), Write Tables to Excel…, Print Graphics…, Preferences, Exit.
  • Edit — Undo/Redo, Cut/Copy/Paste, Delete, transforms (Move, Array, Rotate, Scale, Mirror), Curve to bar / Area to triangle (bake a geometry object into real elements), Select All, Find Entity.
  • Structure — Project Info; Materials, Sections (Bar / Area), Spectral Functions, Fields; and the geometry entries: Nodes (+ Node Springs, coincident-node check/merge), Bars (+ Bar Springs), Triangles, Objects (segment, arc, multisegment, rectangle, polygon), Supports, Constraints, Model check, and Add model from file (merge a second model, welding coincident nodes).
  • Loads — submenus for Point, Distributed, Edge, Settlement and Temperature (bars / areas) loads, each with Manage… and Add…; plus Load Cases.
  • Analysis — Analysis Cases, Combinations, Auto Comb. (EN1990); Cuts (Add cut…, Manage cuts…, Results… — see Results → Cuts); Generate mesh (F6), Model info, Run (F5), Lock (Ctrl+L); plus Variants Workspace… (which includes the Sequences tab) when the variants & construction sequences feature is available.
  • Design — Code preferences, Design combinations, Buckling lengths…, then Concrete Members (ULS/SLS), Concrete Areas (ULS), Steel Members (ULS), Timber Members (ULS), and Punching. See Design.
  • Scene — switch, create, rename, delete Scenes.
  • Selection — Select all / by…, Previous, Invert, Clear, Edit selected nodes / bars / triangles, Divide bars.
  • View — View mode, panel and tool-bar visibility toggles, and Navigate to… (Alt+1 … Alt+7) for the input panels that the canvas and Find Entity do not already reach: supports, springs, materials, sections, loads, combinations, analysis cases.
  • Help — Documentation (F1), Keyboard Shortcuts, About.

docs.title: Left tabs
docs.text:
• Geometry — Nodes, Elements, Supports, Springs, Constraints.
  • Properties — Materials, Sections.
  • Loads — Loads, Analysis Cases, Combinations.
  • Analysis — Results, Design.

Hide or show the whole panel with View → Tables panel (F9).

The left dock also hosts on-demand workbench tabs that open beside Tables / Assistant:

  • Punching — the column list and its actions (plate models). See Design.
  • Buckling — opened by Design → Buckling lengths…, a read-only table of the selected members where you assign the per-member buckling-length factors K. It closes with its own OK button. See Design → Buckling lengths.
  • Cuts — opened by Analysis → Cuts → Results…: cut and case selectors, the Bars/Areas/Total resultant table, and the distribution plot with CSV export. See Results → Cuts.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text: File → Preferences is organised in tabs: General, Display, Design and Colors. The Display tab holds the display sizing defaults (text, marker and line sizes) and the persistent style defaults — the colour map for each field, the default number of levels, continuous vs. banded fill, smoothing, and the bar-diagram and utilisation-ratio styling. The Design tab holds the default design code per material (concrete, steel, timber), whose options come from the same registry as Design → Code preferences; a code stored inside an opened .x2d takes precedence over this default.

docs.title: Display panel
docs.text:
A dockable Display panel (toggle with View → Display panel) has two tabs.

Model — layer visibility: what is drawn in the scene. Node markers and labels, bars and bar labels, areas (triangles/quads) with their borders and labels, objects, support and spring markers, cuts, and the grid (with spacing and snap). In the deformed and modal views an Undeformed structure toggle draws the reference geometry behind the deformed shape. When the model has geometry objects, the Structure view gains a Mesh checkbox that overlays the finite-element mesh generated from those objects (visual only — picking stays on the objects). Reset display turns the layers back on.

Style — live, session-only styling of the active view, in two sections:

  • Colour maps — the colour map of the active view's field. Stresses/forces, shell reinforcement, plate displacements, scalar fields and pressure / temperature loads each keep their own colour map, chosen from one curated, science-friendly list (perceptually-uniform, diverging and sequential palettes, each shown with a preview swatch; no rainbow maps). Also here: continuous vs. discrete (banded) fill, number of levels, contour lines, nodal smoothing, and a manual colour-scale range. The section is enabled only in views that actually draw a colour-mapped field.
  • Diagrams — styling for the bar views. For force diagrams (M/V/N): positive / negative colours, fill opacity, line width, filled band vs. outline, and value labels. For utilisation-ratio colouring (steel / timber design): the colour scheme (traffic-light green→red, or any colour map), the pass/fail threshold, the over-limit colour and the bar width. Each sub-panel is enabled only for the view it applies to.

At the bottom, Save style… / Load style… / Set as default export or import the whole visualization style (colour maps, diagram and ratio styling, and the colour registry) as a portable .json preset, or persist the current style as the startup default. Ready-made presets (publication, presentation, colorblind-safe, grayscale, high-contrast, blueprint) ship in the repository's styles/ folder.

Changes made in the Style tab apply only for the current session; the persistent defaults live in Preferences ▸ Display (and Set as default writes the current style there).

docs.title: Validação/verificação de JSON — mapa e proposta de homogeneização
docs.text: Levantamento de todos os pontos onde a aplicação faz parsing, reparação ou verificação de JSON de modelos, e proposta para os convergir. Nenhuma alteração de código foi feita — este documento é só o diagnóstico.

docs.title: Os dois pontos de entrada
docs.text:
Há dois caminhos por onde um modelo JSON entra na aplicação, e cada um usa um conjunto disjunto de verificações:

  1. Abrir um ficheiro .json na GUI — main_window._load_file.
  2. Extrair um modelo da resposta do assistente (textbox do LLM) — painel do assistente / ai_context.

docs.title: 1. structure_io.load_structure_json → _from_dict (estrito)
docs.text: json.load puro e constrói; rebenta na primeira chave/erro. Loader "programático". src/xdfem2d/structure_io.py:25

docs.title: 2. structure_io_checked.load_structure_json_checked (ficheiro, tolerante)
docs.text: É o que o _load_file usa de facto ao abrir um .json (main_window.py:7853). Contém: - _parse_with_recovery + _try_fix — reparação heurística de sintaxe ao nível do caractere: vírgula pendente, delimitadores ,/: em falta, caracteres soltos, acumulando vários erros. Não remove comentários. - _build_resilient — reconstrói secção a secção (espelhando _from_dict), apanha cada linha má e produz um LoadReport estruturado (LoadIssue com severity/section/index), renderizado por format_report.

docs.title: 3. model_json.parse (LLM, tolerante)
docs.text: Outra reparação, diferente: json.loads, e em falha remove comentários (_strip_comments, // e /* */) e vírgulas finais (regex), e tenta de novo. Não faz recuperação de delimitadores nem acumula erros. src/xdfem2d/model_json.py:584

docs.title: 4. model_json.missing_pieces (verificação semântica sobre o dict)
docs.text: Regras à mão que devolvem frases em prosa: presença das chaves obrigatórias, o par supports/support_assignments, referências penduradas, objetos de geometria, constraints. src/xdfem2d/model_json.py:326

docs.title: 5. model_json.load
docs.text: parse + _from_dict (reutiliza o construtor estrito — aborta ao 1.º erro).

docs.title: 6. ai_context.check_model (ferramenta exposta ao LLM)
docs.text: Usa json.loads estrito (não MJ.parse), depois MJ.load, e reporta opens/missing. src/xdfem2d_app/ai_context.py:2264

docs.title: 7. ai_context._json_candidates + model_in_reply (deteção no textbox)
docs.text: Extrai candidatos (blocos com fence, texto sem fences, slice entre { e }), usa MJ.parse (tolerante) por candidato, filtra por chaves "de modelo", e testa abertura com MJ.load + missing_pieces. src/xdfem2d_app/ai_context.py:2316, 2357. O botão "abrir modelo" do painel usa model_json.load (panels.py:3862).

docs.title: 8. Structure2D.reference_problems() (refs penduradas sobre o objeto)
docs.text: Corre sobre o Structure2D já construído. Chamado no caminho de ficheiro via _warn_reference_problems (main_window.py:7873, 3046) e no botão _model_check (main_window.py:3061).

docs.title: 9. model_check() (topologia, manual)
docs.text: Verificação de topologia (nós livres, coincidentes, T-junctions, etc.), chamada pelo botão _model_check, combinada com reference_problems().

docs.title: O problema
docs.text:
Os mesmos defeitos são tratados por implementações paralelas e disjuntas:

  • Sintaxe tolerante duplicada e assimétrica: o caminho de ficheiro repara delimitadores mas não comentários; o caminho do LLM remove comentários mas não repara delimitadores. O mesmo texto pode abrir num caminho e falhar no outro.
  • Auto-check mais estrito que a deteção passiva: check_model (chamado pelo LLM) usa json.loads estrito, enquanto model_in_reply usa MJ.parse tolerante. Um modelo com comentários passa em model_in_reply mas falha em check_model.
  • Refs penduradas verificadas duas vezes, em domínios diferentes: missing_pieces sobre o dict (caminho LLM) e reference_problems() sobre o objeto construído (caminho ficheiro). Cobertura sobreposta mas não idêntica; cada ponto de entrada só chama uma.
  • Resiliência assimétrica: abrir de ficheiro é resiliente (_build_resilient carrega o que é válido e salta o mau); abrir do LLM usa _from_dict estrito que aborta ao 1.º erro.
  • Completude só para o LLM: abrir um ficheiro nunca corre missing_pieces — um .json incompleto aberto de disco não recebe o aviso.

docs.title: Matriz das assimetrias
docs.text: Sintaxe tolerante Erros de build Refs penduradas Completude Abrir .json _parse_with_recovery (delimitadores, sem comentários) _build_resilient (LoadReport) reference_problems() (sobre objeto) — nunca corre missing_pieces Modelo do LLM model_json.parse (comentários, sem delimitadores) _from_dict estrito (aborta) missing_pieces (sobre dict) missing_pieces

docs.title: Proposta de homogeneização
docs.text:
Convergir para uma camada única de cada tipo, chamada de forma idêntica nos dois pontos de entrada:

  1. Um só parser tolerante. Fundir _strip_comments + vírgulas finais de model_json.parse com o loop _try_fix/_parse_with_recovery de structure_io_checked (comentários → vírgulas finais → recuperação de delimitadores, com acumulação de erros). Ambos os caminhos passam a chamá-lo.

  2. check_model e model_in_reply usam o mesmo parser (o tolerante), para o auto-check do LLM não ser mais estrito que a deteção passiva.

  3. Um só construtor resiliente. model_json.load (e portanto model_in_reply e o botão de abrir do painel) passa a usar _build_resilient/LoadReport em vez de _from_dict estrito, para que modelos do LLM ganhem a mesma recuperação parcial e o mesmo relatório que os ficheiros.

  4. Uma só verificação de referências penduradas. Escolher reference_problems() (sobre o objeto construído — vê o que foi realmente carregado) como canónica; a parte de refs de missing_pieces fica redundante. Ambos os caminhos constroem com _build_resilient e depois correm reference_problems().

  5. Completude nos dois caminhos. A parte de presença de chaves de missing_pieces passa a correr também ao abrir ficheiro, não só para o LLM.

  6. Um formato de relatório único (LoadReport/LoadIssue), alimentado por build-errors + reference_problems() + completude, consumido tanto pelo diálogo de abertura de ficheiro como pelo painel do assistente.

docs.title: Resultado
docs.text: Um parser tolerante, um builder resiliente, uma verificação de referências (sobre o objeto), uma de completude, um relatório — os cinco chamados de forma idêntica nos dois pontos de entrada.

docs.title: O que fica, o que é absorvido
docs.text:
A homogeneização não faz desaparecer o load_structure_json_checked — pelo contrário, ele passa a ser o núcleo partilhado. O que muda:

  • Fica load_structure_json_checked(path) como a assinatura pública "abre um ficheiro e dá-me o relatório". Deixa apenas de ser o único sítio onde a construção resiliente existe.
  • Fica _build_resilient / LoadReport — passa a ser também o construtor do caminho do LLM.
  • Fica _from_dict estrito — legítimo para uso programático; só deixa de ser o construtor do caminho do LLM.
  • É absorvido o mini-parser tolerante de model_json.parse: funde-se com _parse_with_recovery num parser único (o _parse_with_recovery ganha o _strip_comments).
  • Fica redundante a parte de referências de missing_pieces, face a reference_problems() sobre o objeto construído.

docs.title: Onde vive a lógica unificada — recomendação
docs.text:
Recomenda-se a hipótese 1: structure_io_checked continua a ser a casa.

  • structure_io_checked fica dono de tudo o que é "dict/ficheiro → Structure2D + LoadReport". Ganha uma variante que aceita um dict já parseado, ex. build_checked(data) -> (struc, report). O load_structure_json_checked(path) passa a ser uma casca fina: lê o ficheiro, parseia (parser tolerante unificado) e chama build_checked.
  • model_json fica com o que é dele: template, parser tolerante (partilhado), extração de texto (_json_candidates/model_in_reply) e completude. Para construir, delega em structure_io_checked.build_checked.

Porquê a 1 e não a 2 (pôr a construção resiliente dentro de model_json):

  • Responsabilidades. Construir um Structure2D a partir de um dict é do domínio do loader de estruturas, não do módulo do assistente. A hipótese 2 daria ao model_json duas responsabilidades e forçaria o "checked loader" a depender do model_json.
  • Direção da dependência. Com a 1, aponta na direção natural: model_json → structure_io_checked → structure. O caminho do assistente é um cliente do loader, não o contrário.
  • Custo. O único custo face à 2 é uma função pública a mais (build_checked) — barato e até desejável: dá um ponto de teste isolado para a construção resiliente, sem passar por ficheiro nem por texto de LLM.

docs.title: Loads
docs.text: All loads belong to a load case. A load case is purely a definition of loads — it does not produce results on its own; an analysis case solves it.

docs.title: Load cases
docs.text:
Create load cases on the Loads tab. A load case has:

  • a name,
  • a self-weight multiplier (e.g. 1.0 to include full self-weight, 0.0 to exclude it), and
  • an action type (G permanent, Q live, W wind, E seismic, T temperature) used by the automatic Eurocode combination generator.

Note

Adding a load case automatically creates a matching Linear analysis case of the same name (factor 1.0), so the load case can be solved and combined right away.

docs.title: Load types
docs.text:
Load Applies to Parameters Point load a node Fx, Fy, Mz Distributed load an element trapezoidal Fy/Fx start→end, global or local axes Element point load a point along an element Fx, Fy, Mz at distance a Edge load a triangle edge or a surface boundary side traction Fx, Fy per unit length Temperature (bars) an element uniform ΔT and gradient ΔT Temperature (areas) a triangle uniform ΔT over the element Support settlement a supported node prescribed ux, uy, θz Nodal mass a node (for a Mass case) Mx, My, Mtz

Add each from its sub-table on the Loads tab, or from the Loads menu (Manage… / Add… per type), selecting the load case it belongs to. The component names above are the plane-domain ones; the dialogs read them in the active domain's terms (see below and Domains).

Edge loads are the surface-element counterpart of a distributed load: pick the two end nodes of a triangle edge or a surface boundary side — the Add edge load tool lets you click them on the canvas — and give the traction per unit length. They are the way to apply pressure to a wall or plate.

docs.title: In the plate domain
docs.text:
A slab or grillage bends out of plane, so its loads are transverse (see Slabs and Grillages):

  • Point load — Fz (transverse force), Mx, My (moments).
  • Distributed load on a grillage beam — a transverse intensity qz.
  • Area pressure pz [kN/m²] on a slab region (a surface object or a single triangle) — the everyday slab load, drawn as a colour map over the region. Add it from Loads → Area Pressure (Manage… / Add…).
  • Winkler area spring kz [kN/m³] — a slab on grade, lumped kz·A/3 at each triangle vertex. It is a support, not a load, but is applied over a region the same way.
  • Area temperature — a slab does not stretch, it bends, so a triangle or surface temperature is the through-thickness gradient ΔT = T_top − T_bottom, which curves the plate element (a uniform rise is stress-free).

Field temperatures need the mesh

A field-driven temperature on a surface object only resolves once the object is meshed into triangles. Before that the loads view shows a note asking you to Generate mesh (F6); a constant pressure or gradient draws immediately.

docs.title: Self-weight
docs.text: Self-weight is applied per load case through its self-weight multiplier, using each element's section area and material unit weight. There is no separate self-weight load to add — set the multiplier on the load case.

docs.title: Viewing loads
docs.text: Switch the View dropdown to Loads and pick a load case (or all load cases) to draw arrows and value labels on the canvas.

docs.title: Modelling the Structure
docs.text: Build a model from the Geometry and Properties tabs, or directly on the canvas. The model must be unlocked to edit (toggle with Ctrl+L); running an analysis locks it.

docs.title: Materials and sections
docs.text:
Define these first, on the Properties tab.

  • Material — elastic modulus E (kN/m²), unit weight γ (kN/m³), and thermal expansion α (1/°C).

  • Section — a cross-section linked to a material. A Shape field selects the geometry and which dimensions are needed; the area and second moment of area are derived automatically and shown as read-only labels:

    Shape Dimensions used Generic b × h (or a steel-profile override) Rectangular width b, height h Circular diameter d Rectangular hollow b × h, wall thickness t Circular hollow diameter d, wall thickness t I flange width b, total height h, flange tf, web tw T flange width b, total height h, flange tf, web tw

    A steel profile picked from the library still fills the area/inertia directly. The separate Type field (Concrete / Steel / Timber / Other) is for material /design classification and is independent of the shape.

Built-in Rigid and Dummy

Every model is seeded with two reserved entries — a material and a section — called Rigid (numerically very stiff, for near-rigid links) and Dummy (zero stiffness, for a member that must be otherwise restrained). They are opened read-only, cannot be renamed or deleted, and are shown at the bottom of the material and section lists.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
A node has an (x, y) position. Add nodes from the Nodes sub-tab, the Structure menu, or with the Add node tool: enable it and click on the canvas to place nodes; press Esc to stop.

Double-click a node on the canvas to edit its position, support, or spring.

docs.title: Elements
docs.text:
An element's role follows from what it spans and the model's domain: a line element is a Beam in a plane model and a Grid member in a plate model; an area element — a triangle or a quad — is a Panel in a plane model and a Slab in a plate model. The tabs, menus and section dialogs use these names, so the same primitives read correctly in either domain.

A bar element connects two nodes and references a section. Add elements from the Beams / Grid sub-tab or with the Add element tool: enable it, click the start node, then the end node.

Each element end can carry a moment release (hinge), drawn as a small open circle near the node.

docs.title: Triangle (surface) elements
docs.text:
For membranes, walls and plates in plane stress or plane strain, xdfem2D uses triangular surface elements. A triangle section carries a thickness, a material, a plane-stress/plane-strain flag, and a formulation:

Formulation DOFs per node Notes CST (constant-strain triangle) ux, uy Fast, robust; overly stiff in bending. The node's rotation is left free (auto-restrained) unless a bar also frames in. Allman ux, uy, θz Adds an in-plane drilling rotation, so it can transfer moment to a frame member and converges faster in bending. ES-FEM (edge-based smoothed) ux, uy Smooths CST over edge domains — softer, more accurate in bending — without adding a DOF.

Add triangles one by one (three node picks) on the Triangles sub-tab, or let a polygon geometry object mesh itself automatically.

docs.title: Quadrilateral (surface) elements
docs.text:
A quad is the 4-node counterpart of the triangle, for the same walls and slabs. Its main advantage is on a regular, structured mesh (a rectangular slab or wall panel): a triangle split introduces a directional (diagonal) bias in the stress/moment field near supports and point loads — a checkerboard pattern — that a quad avoids. Prefer quads on regular grids; keep triangles for irregular or concave outlines (the quad mesher is structured-only).

A quad section carries the same thickness / material / plane-strain fields as a triangle section, with its own formulation:

Formulation Domain Notes QM6 (incompatible-modes Q4) plane (wall) The recommended membrane quad — four internal bubble DOFs, condensed out, fix the bending-lock that plain Q4 suffers. Q4 (bilinear) plane (wall) Reference/patch-test element only — locks in bending, not recommended as the default. MITC4 (Mindlin, shear-locking-free) plate (slab) The recommended slab quad — the 4-node analogue of MITC3. DKT4 (thin, Kirchhoff) plate (slab) Four DKT triangles condensed to a quad; thin-plate analogue of DKT.

Add quads one by one (four node picks, i → j → k → l counter-clockwise) from Structure ▸ Triangles ▸ Add quad, or let a rectangle/polygon object mesh into quads (below). A triangle and a quad are the same modelling role, so they share one selection, one Manage area elements… manager, one bulk/individual editor, and the same result views — pick the shape per element or per surface.

Panel sections

In the GUI a Panel pairs a triangle section and a quad section under one name (one material/thickness choice), and the surface's Mesh as: Triangles / Quads selector decides which is used. Programmatically they are two sections (tri_sections / quad_sections) that may share a name.

docs.title: Geometry objects (parametric)
docs.text:
Instead of placing every node and element by hand, you can define the structure with parametric geometry objects that the program discretises into concrete nodes and elements at solve time. The editable model is left untouched; the analysis runs on the compiled mesh.

Object Becomes Defined by Segment bar elements two end points Arc bar elements (straight chords) centre + radius + angles, or three points Multisegment bar elements a chain of vertices, open or closed Rectangle triangle or quad mesh two opposite corners Polygon triangle or quad mesh a closed polygon boundary

Polygons and rectangles are meshed by an automatic Delaunay mesher (the built-in one, or the higher-quality Triangle library if installed) into triangles, or — on a convex quad outline with Mesh as: Quads and a quad section — by the structured mesher into quads (falling back to triangles per cell where a quad would be poorly shaped). When the model is analysed, objects auto-resolve T-junctions and crossings: a node sitting on another object's span, or two objects that cross, are welded so the parts act together.

Create objects from Structure ▸ Objects (segment / arc / multisegment / rectangle / polygon). To turn an object into ordinary elements you can edit individually, use Edit ▸ Curve to bar or Edit ▸ Surface to mesh (which bakes the surface into its triangles and/or quads).

Propagation along an edge

Supports and springs assigned to both corner nodes of a meshed edge propagate to the intermediate nodes the mesher creates along that edge. This is how you fix a whole wall base with two assignments instead of forty.

docs.title: Supports
docs.text:
Supports restrain node degrees of freedom — ux, uy, θz in a plane model, w, θx, θy in a plate model (see Domains). Each restraint combination has a canonical name, so the same boundary condition is called the same thing whether it was drawn or written by script, and the canvas draws an expressive glyph per family. The name depends on the domain:

Restraints Plane name Plate name all three FIXED CLAMPED two translations / w only PIN SIMPLE one only ROLLER-X / ROLLER-Y SYM-X / SYM-Y translation + one rotation GUIDED-X / GUIDED-Y CLAMP-X / CLAMP-Y rotation(s), free to move BLOCK BLOCK

In the plate domain the glyphs read as slab edges: a simply-supported knife-edge (SIMPLE), a hatched clamp (CLAMPED), a supported edge with one rotation held (CLAMP-X/Y), and a dash-dot symmetry line (SYM-X/Y) — the last lets you model a whole slab from one wedge. The quick-preset buttons in the support dialog offer the domain's common cases (plane: PIN / ROLLER-X / FIXED; plate: SIMPLE / CLAMPED / SYM-X).

Assign supports on the Supports sub-tab or via the node editor. The on-canvas legend names each colour with its canonical family (the -X/-Y variants share one entry).

docs.title: Springs
docs.text:
• Node springs — translational Kx, Ky and rotational Kt at a node.
  • Element springs — a Winkler elastic foundation along an element, per unit length.

A structure may be supported by springs alone (no classic supports), as long as the springs restrain enough degrees of freedom to prevent rigid-body motion.

docs.title: Unilateral (tension-/compression-only) springs
docs.text:
Each translational component of a node or element spring has a behaviour mode:

Mode Acts when… Typical use both (default) always — resists in both directions ordinary elastic spring compression the spring is compressed (node moves in the −axis direction) soil under a footing, gap/contact support tension the spring is stretched (node moves in the +axis direction) tie / anchor that only pulls

Set the mode per component (Kx/Ky for global axes, axial/transverse for an element spring in local axes) in the spring dialog, the node/element editor, or the bulk-edit dialog. Rotational stiffness Kt is always bilateral.

Only NonLinear cases honour the mode

Tension-/compression-only behaviour is applied only by a NonLinear analysis case. In Linear (and every other) case the spring acts bilaterally, exactly as before. So model the unilateral effect by running a NonLinear case.

Sign convention: for a node spring the component direction is the global axis (or, for an element spring in local axes, the element's axial / transverse direction). "tension" is active when the displacement projected on that direction is positive; "compression" when it is negative. Element-spring activation is evaluated per end-node, consistent with the lumped foundation model.

Modelling a footing on soil (uplift)

Give the base nodes/elements compression-only springs and remove any rigid vertical supports at those nodes (a rigid support in parallel with a spring fixes the DOF and makes the spring inert). Keep a minimal horizontal restraint to prevent rigid-body motion, then solve with a NonLinear case: the springs that go into tension deactivate and that part of the footing lifts.

docs.title: Constraints (multi-point)
docs.text:
Supports and springs act on one degree of freedom at a time. A constraint instead couples several DOFs — of different nodes — through a linear equation. Three kinds are available, all built from the same underlying form Σ cᵢ·dofᵢ = value:

Kind What it does Rigid link A master node and one or more slave nodes move as one rigid body: each slave follows the master's two translations and rotation (ux_s = ux_m − Δy·θ_m, uy_s = uy_m + Δx·θ_m, θ_s = θ_m). Use it for rigid offsets and eccentric connections. Equal DOF A set of nodes shares the same value of one or more components (ux, uy, θz) — e.g. tying several nodes to the same horizontal displacement. Equation (advanced) The raw linear form: a list of (node, component, coefficient) terms and a right-hand-side value.

Create constraints on the Constraints sub-tab (Geometry), or from Structure ▸ Constraints ▸ Add constraint (also under Structure ▸ Nodes). The Add constraint tool lets you click the nodes to tie on the canvas — each picked node is highlighted — and finishes when you double-click the last node, which opens the editor pre-filled with those nodes. Press Esc to leave the mode. The dialog previews the resulting equation(s) before you save, and gives a default name per kind (Rigid1, Equal1, Constraint1, …).

How constraints are imposed (penalty)

Constraints are enforced by penalty: each equation adds a very stiff term to the stiffness matrix. This is robust and works across all analysis types (Linear, NonLinear, P-Delta, Modal, Spectrum), but it is approximate — results satisfy the constraint to about 1 part in 10⁶, with a tiny residual reaction. An exact master–slave formulation is planned for a future version.

The model check flags common mistakes: a constraint referencing a missing node, a rigid link whose master is also a slave, two rigid links forming a cycle, a tied DOF that a support already restrains, and a constraint on θz at a node with no rotational DOF (CST-only).

See Results ▸ Constraint forces for the force each constraint transmits.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: A field is a named spatial expression — a formula in x and y — that can drive a value which varies across the model instead of a single constant. The main use is a Winkler foundation modulus that changes along a member: assign a field as an element spring's stiffness and the value is evaluated at each generated bar's midpoint. Define fields in Structure ▸ Fields, and preview one over the model with the Fields view mode.

docs.title: Editing on the canvas
docs.text:
• Click to select; drag a rectangle for a window selection (left-to-right encloses, right-to-left crosses).
  • Selection menu / panel: Select all, Invert, Clear, Edit nodes, Edit elements, Delete.
  • Cut/Copy/Paste (Ctrl+X / Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V) duplicate a selection with an offset. Undo/Redo (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y) cover all edits.

docs.title: Transforms and bulk edits
docs.text:
The Edit menu applies geometric transforms to the current selection:

Command Effect Move Translate by a vector Array Replicate along a grid (copies at a spacing, a count in each direction) Rotate Rotate about a point Scale Scale about a point Mirror Reflect across an axis

Two commands bake parametric objects into ordinary, individually-editable elements: Curve to bar (segment / arc / multisegment → bars) and Area to triangle (rectangle / polygon → triangles); the object is then removed.

To change many entities at once, select them and use Selection → Edit selected nodes / bars / triangles… for a bulk editor, or Divide bars… to subdivide selected members into several elements.

docs.title: Checking and meshing the model
docs.text:
• Structure → Model check (also in the Analysis menu) reports topology issues that are not auto-fixed: isolated nodes, coincident nodes, unconnected T-junctions and crossings, duplicate bars, masses on restrained DOFs, and the constraint checks above.
  • Analysis → Generate mesh (F6) compiles the geometry objects into the concrete mesh the solver uses, so you can inspect it before running — it is shown via the Mesh overlay checkbox on the Structure view (Display panel ▸ Model tab), which draws the generated mesh over the geometry objects.
  • Analysis → Model info shows a summary of the model's size and contents.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: After running an analysis (F5), review results on the canvas, in the Results tab, and through the exports.

docs.title: View modes
docs.text:
Switch with the View dropdown, View → View mode, or the Ctrl+1…Ctrl+9 accelerators. The dropdown lists only the modes that have data for the current model, so entries appear and disappear as you mesh, run, or design.

Mode Shortcut Shows Case selector Structure Ctrl+1 Geometry only load cases Loads Ctrl+2 Applied loads load cases Fields A field expression mapped over the model — Modal shapes Ctrl+3 Mode shapes modal cases Deformed shape Ctrl+4 Cubic-Hermite deflected shape analysis cases / sequences / combinations Displacements Nodal-displacement diagram along members analysis cases / sequences / combinations Reactions Ctrl+5 Support reaction arrows + sum analysis cases / sequences / combinations Constraint forces Force each constraint applies at its nodes analysis cases / sequences / combinations Bending moment Ctrl+6 M diagram along members analysis cases / sequences / combinations Shear force Ctrl+7 V diagram analysis cases / sequences / combinations Axial force Ctrl+8 N diagram analysis cases / sequences / combinations Stress (σ) / Forces Triangle field: plane membrane stresses σx, σy, τxy, σ1, σ2, von Mises (kN/m²); plate slab forces mx, my, mxy, m1, m2, vx, vy and Wood–Armer (W-A) design moments (kNm/m) analysis cases / sequences / combinations Reinforcement (As) Ctrl+9 EC2 bar flexural reinforcement envelope design results Shear reinf. (Asw) EC2 bar shear reinforcement design results Shell reinf. (As) EC2 membrane reinforcement of triangles design results Crack width (wk) EC2 SLS crack-width verification design results

The Fields mode requires a compiled mesh; the stress mode needs triangle elements; the reinforcement and crack modes need the matching design run. The analysed mesh itself is inspected via the Mesh overlay checkbox on the Structure view (Display panel ▸ Model tab), not a separate view mode. The Constraint forces mode appears only when the model has constraints.

Only modes with available data are enabled. Use the Case dropdown to pick which analysis case, sequence, or combination to display; for Modal, choose the Mode number. When a construction sequence is selected, a phase selector appears in the toolbar to navigate phase by phase. A Cumulative / Increment toggle controls whether displacements show the running total (Σ Δu) or only the current phase's increment (Δu); forces and reactions always reflect the accumulated state up to the selected phase.

The triangle-field view is domain-aware: its title reads Stress in a plane model and Forces in a plate model, and the component selector lists the matching quantities (σ… vs mx, my, …, W-A). In a plane model a Forces (N=σ·t) checkbox converts the membrane stresses into forces per unit width — Nx, Ny, Nxy, N1, N2 in kN/m, each scaled by the triangle's own thickness (von Mises is omitted, having no force meaning). Plate results are already stress resultants, so no toggle appears there.

docs.title: Scale and undeformed reference
docs.text:
For deformed and diagram views, the Scale spin box sets the magnification. With Auto on, the result is fitted to about 10 % of the model span. In the deformed and modal views, an Undeformed structure checkbox toggles the reference geometry; support markers stay visible if their layer is enabled.

The look of each result view — colour map, banded vs. continuous fill, levels, contour lines, smoothing and colour-scale range for the field views, and the sign colours, opacity, line width and value labels for the M/V/N diagrams and the utilisation-ratio colouring — is set live in the Style tab of the Display panel, and persists via Preferences ▸ Display.

docs.title: Reactions and equilibrium
docs.text:
The Reactions view draws an arrow per support and a corner box with the Σ reactions (ΣRx, ΣRy, ΣMz) — the total support force, which doubles as an equilibrium check against the applied loads.

Spring reactions are drawn too: node springs as labelled arrows, and element (Winkler) foundation springs as a distributed reaction diagram with numeric values (reaction per unit length) at each element end. The colour shows the state — blue for compression (the spring pushes the structure) and red for tension (it pulls). For a NonLinear case the unilateral state is respected: sections where a tension-/compression-only spring is inactive show zero reaction (e.g. the lifted part of a footing carries no soil reaction), instead of the spurious tension a Linear case would draw.

docs.title: Constraint forces
docs.text:
For a model with constraints, the Constraint forces view draws — in magenta — the force each constraint applies at the nodes it couples: an arrow for Fx and Fy and a label for the moment Mz. This is the force you could apply instead of the constraint to get the same displacements: for a rigid link it is the force and moment transmitted through the link; for an equal-DOF tie it is the internal tie force (equal and opposite between the tied nodes).

The value is recovered as the residual of the physical stiffness at the coupled DOFs — the same method used for support reactions — so it is well-conditioned despite the penalty. The same numbers appear in the Constraint forces table of the Results report and the Excel export (only when constraints exist).

docs.title: Cuts
docs.text:
A cut is a straight segment you draw across the model to read the resultant of the internal forces crossing it — bars and areas, combined and separately — for one case or combination at a time. Unlike everything else on this page, a cut needs no re-run when added, renamed or moved: it is a report definition over whatever is already solved.

Analysis → Cuts → Add cut… picks two points on the canvas (any two points, not necessarily nodes) and opens a small dialog for the cut's Name — the only field you set; there is no separate id to manage, and two cuts cannot share a name. Manage cuts… lists every cut with its endpoints for add/edit/delete. Cuts are drawn on the canvas as a plain segment with its name and a short arrow along the normal — the side the arrow points to is the positive side: results are reported as what the positive side exerts on the negative side.

Analysis → Cuts → Results… opens the results side panel: pick a cut and a case/combination, and a table shows the resultant in three rows — Bars, Areas, Total — with columns N, V, M for a plane cut (axial along the cut's normal, shear along its tangent, in-plane moment about the cut's midpoint) or V, Mb, Mt for a plate cut (transverse shear, bending and twisting moment — the same mn/mnt split the triangle stress view uses). Below the table, a small plot shows the chosen per-length area field along the cut, with a marker at every point a bar crosses it. Export CSV… writes the same table for the selected case, or every case at once, to a spreadsheet-ready file.

See dev/CUT_PLAN.md for the sign conventions and engine-api.md for the Python API (xdfem2d.cuts.cut_result and friends) if you are scripting against a model instead of using the GUI.

docs.title: The Results report
docs.text:
The Results tab (Analysis → Results) prints a full text report:

  • per load case, combination and analysis case: displacements, reactions (with a Σ row), and element end-forces;
  • element span extremes (|N|max, |V|max, M⁺, M⁻);
  • modal tables with frequency, period, effective mass per mode and the running cumulative mass (ΣX%, ΣY%).

docs.title: Exports
docs.text:
• Write Report… (Ctrl+Shift+W) — a PDF, Word, or Excel report; pick the format and the content (tables, drawings, result views per case).
  • Write Tables to Excel… (Ctrl+Shift+T) — one-click workbook of the model and result tables (Displacements, Reactions, Constraint forces, Element forces, Span extremes, Reaction sums, Modal). The Constraint-forces sheet appears only when the model has constraints.

See Exporting.

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
A Scene is a named, saved subset of the model — a chosen set of nodes and elements. While a scene is active, the canvas behaves as if only those members exist: rendering, hit-testing, window selection, viewport-fit, and the loads/diagrams/ reactions overlays are all confined to the scene.

Scenes are saved inside the .x2d file, and each remembers its own zoom.

docs.title: Switching scenes
docs.text: Use the Scene menu or the Scene dropdown in the tool bar. Full model shows everything; selecting a scene confines the view to its members and restores that scene's saved zoom.

docs.title: Creating and editing
docs.text:
From the Scene menu:

  • New scene from selection… — select nodes/elements, then create a named scene from them.
  • Add selection to scene ▸ — add the current selection to a chosen scene. This is typically done from Full model, where you can freely select objects outside any scene.
  • Remove selection from scene — drop the current selection from the active scene.
  • Update scene to selection — replace the active scene's members with the current selection.
  • Rename scene… / Delete scene.

docs.title: Behaviour with edits
docs.text:
• New geometry created while a scene is active (add node/element, paste) joins the active scene so it stays visible.
  • Deleting geometry removes it from all scenes automatically; undo/redo keep scenes consistent with the model.

docs.title: Slabs and Grillages
docs.text:
A plate model bends out of plane: a slab (plate-bending triangles) or a grillage (beams carrying transverse load and torsion). It is one of the two model domains; pick Slab / Grillage (out-of-plane) in New model. The DOFs per node are w, θx, θy.

This page is the orientation for plate models. The everyday topics — supports, loads, analysis, results, design — are covered for both domains on their own pages, linked below.

docs.title: What is plate-specific
docs.text: Topic Plate specifics Where Sections Plate section = material + thickness t + element (MITC3 shear-deformable, the default; DKT thin-plate); grillage beam reuses the bar section and gains a St-Venant torsion constant J = β·b·h³ (with G = E/2(1+ν)) Modelling Supports restrain w, θx, θy: SIMPLE, CLAMPED, CLAMP-X/Y, SYM-X/Y (symmetry lines) Modelling Loads point Fz, Mx, My; beam qz; area pressure pz; Winkler kz; through-thickness thermal gradient ΔT Loads Analysis linear, non-linear, modal and spectrum — vertical modes; no P-Delta Analysis Results deflection field w/θx/θy; slab forces mx, my, mxy, m1, m2, vx, vy; Wood–Armer (W-A) design moments; grillage M/V/T diagrams; reactions Rz, Mx, My Results Templates Slabs (rectangular slab, rib-stiffened, flat slab on columns, on grade, circular sector) and Grillages (beam grid, bridge deck) Templates

docs.title: By script
docs.text:
The engine reaches all of this without the interface:

from xdfem2d import Structure2D

s = Structure2D(domain='plate')
s.add_material('C30/37', elastic_modulus=33e6, unit_weight=25.0, poisson=0.2)
s.add_plate_section('SLAB', 'C30/37', thickness=0.20)      # MITC3 (default; formulation='DKT' for thin plates)
s.add_quad_section('SLABQ', 'C30/37', thickness=0.20, formulation='MITC4')  # quad slab (DKT4 for thin)
s.add_section('BEAM', 'C30/37', b=0.3, h=0.5)              # grillage (gains J)
# ... nodes, then triangles (add_tri_element, 3 nodes) and/or
#     quads (add_quad_element, 4 ccw nodes), and/or bars ...
s.add_support('SS', w=True)
s.add_area_load('S1', 'LC', pz=-10.0)   # pz targets a triangle OR a quad id (or a surface object)
r = s.calculate()

docs.title: Slab element: MITC3 vs DKT (and their quad twins)
docs.text:
A slab triangle uses one of two plate-bending elements, chosen per section:

  • MITC3 (the default) is shear-deformable (Mindlin–Reissner): it accounts for transverse-shear deflection, so it is valid for thick slabs as well as thin ones and reports a genuine shear field vx, vy. It converges to the exact Mindlin solution and passes the constant-moment patch test.
  • DKT is the thin-plate (Kirchhoff) element: no shear deformation, very accurate for thin slabs on coarse meshes.

Use the default (MITC3) unless the slab is very thin and the mesh is coarse, where DKT converges with fewer elements. Both share the same nodes, DOFs, results and Wood–Armer design moments, so switching is just the section's formulation.

A slab can also be meshed with quads on a regular grid, which avoid the diagonal bias a triangle split introduces near supports and point loads. The quad slab elements are the 4-node twins of the two triangles, chosen the same way on a quad section:

  • MITC4 — the shear-locking-free Mindlin quad, the 4-node analogue of MITC3 (the recommended slab quad).
  • DKT4 — the thin-plate quad (four DKT triangles condensed), the analogue of DKT.

They carry the same moments/shears, Wood–Armer design and result views as the triangles, so a mixed tri/quad slab (quads in the regular field, triangles at an irregular edge) is one continuous model. See Quadrilateral elements for how to create them and the "prefer quads on a regular grid" guidance.

Runnable examples live in examples/example-slab.py (thin slab with the DKT element, checked against the Kirchhoff Navier series), examples/example-slab-mitc3.py (thick slab with the MITC3 element, checked against the exact Mindlin series — the transverse-shear deflection the DKT misses), examples/example-grillage.py (crossed two-beam grillage, load split) and examples/example-grillage-cantilever.py (cantilever bar checked against the bending F·L³/3EI and the St-Venant torsion T·L/GJ).

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
File → New from Template… (Ctrl+T) generates a ready-made model. Pick a Category and then a Type, set the geometry parameters and the common material/section properties, and watch the live preview update as you type; click OK to draw the structure onto the canvas.

The dialog is organised into three titled, consistently indented boxes — Geometry, Material and Section — followed by the live preview. Each box adjusts its height to the fields the current type needs.

docs.title: Available templates
docs.text:
Templates are grouped into six families, in this order: Beams & Frames, Slabs, Walls, Trusses, Grillages, Arches. Beams & Frames, Walls, Trusses and Arches build plane models; Slabs and Grillages build plate models (out-of-plane bending — see Slabs and Grillages).

Beams & Frames

Type Parameters Description Continuous beam spans, span length, left / intermediate / right support Multi-span beam with an independent support condition at each position Portal span, height Single-bay, single-storey, fixed bases Rectangular bays, floors, bay width, floor height Multi-bay, multi-storey, fixed bases

The continuous beam replaces the old single-span beam types: pick the support at the left end, the intermediate supports and the right end — each Free, Pin (canonical PIN) or Fixed (canonical FIXED). The intermediate combo is disabled for a single span. The span length accepts a single value (uniform spans) or a comma-separated list such as 6, 5, 4 for variable spans; a list overrides the number of spans.

Both bay width and floor height (frames) accept a single value or a comma-separated list (e.g. 5, 4, 6 widths, 4, 3, 3 heights) for variable spacing; a list overrides the corresponding bays / floors count. In parametric-object mode the rectangular frame emits one object per column (spanning the full height) and one object per floor beam (spanning the full length), welded to the joint nodes.

Trusses

Trusses use the same shaped bar section as beams and frames (not just an area).

Type Parameters Description King post panels, span, depth King-post truss; an odd panel count inverts the diagonals so it differs from the next even count Warren panels, span, depth Triangulated, no verticals (symmetric for any panel count) Howe panels, span, depth Verticals + diagonals sloping to centre; even panels only (odd would be asymmetric) Pratt panels, span, depth Verticals + diagonals (tension under gravity); even panels only Long (X-braced) panels, span, depth Howe + Pratt superimposed — a full X of diagonals in every panel (statically indeterminate); symmetric for any panel count Town lattice span, depth, diagonal pitch, lattice span k Dense crossing lattice: diagonals jump k panels, spaced by the pitch (rounded to fit the span), joined only at the chords, with end posts

For Howe and Pratt the panel spinbox steps in twos (a single diagonal per panel cannot be mirror-symmetric with an odd count). Warren and Long are symmetric for any count; King post keeps the full range and inverts its diagonals for an odd panel count. The Town lattice density is set by the diagonal pitch (target chord-node spacing, rounded so a whole number of panels fits the span) and the lattice span k (how many panels each diagonal jumps).

Arches

Type Parameters Description Parabolic (two-hinged) segments, span, rise Two-hinged parabolic arch

Walls

Type Parameters Description Wall panel width, height, mesh X/Y Rectangular plane-stress panel meshed in triangles, fixed along its base Deep beam width (span), height (depth), mesh X/Y Plane-stress panel supported at its two bottom corners (pin + roller) Wall + Frame bays, floors, bay width, floor height, wall width, wall mesh X, wall side Rectangular frame with a full-height shear wall at one end

Wall + Frame combines a rectangular frame with a plane-stress wall on the chosen wall side (Left / Right). The wall spans the full frame height and is meshed in modules aligned with the floor levels, so its interface nodes coincide with — and share — the frame's floor joints (the wall connects to the frame at every floor). It uses a single (concrete) material and a combined section giving both the frame bar dimensions (b, h) and the wall thickness / formulation. Bay width and floor height accept lists for variable spacing. Both frame bases and the wall base are fixed.

Every wall (and every slab) offers a Mesh element choice — Triangle or Quadrilateral — and an Element formulation whose options follow that choice: membrane triangles ES-FEM / Allman / CST or quads QM6 / Q4 for walls; plate triangles MITC3 / DKT or quads MITC4 / DKT4 for slabs.

Slabs (plate domain)

Type Parameters Description Rectangular slab Lx, Ly, mesh element/formulation, thickness, per-edge support Rectangular slab with an independent condition on each edge — Free, Pin (SIMPLE) or Fixed (CLAMPED), using the canonical plate support names Rib-stiffened Lx, Ly, mesh element/formulation, slab t, rib b/h Slab with edge beams (grillage ribs), resting on the corners Flat slab on columns bay Lx, Ly (value or list), column bays X/Y, max element size, thickness Slab carried only on a grid of columns (point W supports), no edge beams. Lx/Ly are the bay span — a single value (uniform bays) or a list like 6, 4, 6 for variable bays; columns land exactly on every bay line and each bay is meshed to the given max element size On grade (Winkler) Lx, Ly, mesh element/formulation, thickness, kz Slab on an elastic foundation (subgrade kz), the springs alone carry it Circular sector rmin, rmax, θ, max element size, thickness, per-edge support Circular slab sector with an independent condition on each edge — outer arc, inner arc and the two radial sides — each Free / Pin (SIMPLE) / Fixed (CLAMPED). rmin = 0 gives a solid sector (no inner arc), θ = 360 a full disc (no radial sides). The curved boundary is faceted and filled with a quality unstructured mesh at the given max element size

Grillages (plate domain — beam grids)

Type Parameters Description Beam grid Lx, Ly, bays X/Y, beam b/h Orthogonal grillage, simply supported on the perimeter Bridge deck span L, width W, girders, transverse stations, girder b/h, transverse b/h Longitudinal girders tied by transverse diaphragms, simply supported at the two abutments

A slab section is a thickness plus the chosen plate element (Triangle MITC3/DKT or Quadrilateral MITC4/DKT4); a grillage beam reuses the shaped bar section and gains a torsion constant J. All plate templates seed a self-weight load case; the slabs also carry a uniform area pressure pz.

docs.title: Material and Section
docs.text:
Below the Geometry box are two more, laid out in two columns each:

  • Material — pick a type (Concrete / Steel / Timber) and a grade (C25/30, S275, C24…), shown side by side. The preset sets E, γ and ν; fine-tune them later in the material editor.
  • Section — adapts to the family and material:
    • for beams, frames, arches and trusses, the bar section depends on the material type. Concrete and Timber show only b and h (with sensible defaults — concrete 0.30 × 0.50 m, timber 0.12 × 0.36 m). Steel shows only a rolled I-profile dropdown (HEA/HEB/HEM/IPE, IPE100 by default) whose dimensions define the section;
    • thickness t, the Mesh element (Triangle / Quadrilateral) and the matching Element formulation for walls and slabs;
    • a combined section (frame b/h + wall thickness / formulation) for Wall + Frame.

docs.title: Parametric objects (auto-meshed)
docs.text: For Beams & Frames, Arches, Walls and Slabs, a checkbox Create as parametric objects (auto-meshed) makes the template emit geometry objects — lines / a polyline for the bar families, rectangles for walls (one per floor module in Wall + Frame), a rectangle/polygon for slabs — instead of explicit nodes and elements. The objects discretise into elements at solve time, so the model stays parametric and easy to re-mesh or edit. The wall's mesh divisions then set the target element size. Trusses have no single-object form and keep the explicit output.

docs.title: What every template includes
docs.text:
• A self-weight load case named SW with self-weight multiplier 1.0.
  • A Linear analysis case, also named SW, that applies it with factor 1.0.

So a template is ready to Run (F5) immediately and show its self-weight response. Add further load cases, analysis cases, and combinations as needed — see Loads and Analysis.

docs.title: Variants & Construction Sequences
docs.text: Two related features let you study a structure under parallel scenarios and under a staged construction sequence, both accessible from the same workspace and integrated into the normal analysis flow.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
A variant is a what-if overlay on the working model: the same shared geometry, but with a chosen subset of active elements and an optional support set (a named collection of node restraints). The base model is never mutated — each variant is resolved into a derived structure only when it is solved.

Open Analysis → Variants Workspace… for a single window with four tabs:

  • Variants — create and edit variants (id, description, support set, active elements). A variant with All elements checked keeps the full geometry and follows any base changes automatically. Use the Sync with base button to pull in geometry changes and review what has changed.
  • Support sets — define reusable restraint sets (per-node UX/UY/TZ), for example a "provisional supports" set used by a variant or a construction phase.
  • Combine — combine the results of several variants with the same arithmetic as a load combination (a list of variant × case × factor terms and an operation). Use it to compare or superpose scenarios.
  • Sequences — define and run construction sequences (see below).

Once variants exist, a variant selector appears in the tool bar. Picking a variant shows its model and results in the normal editors and views. Variant models stay in sync with the base automatically: geometry and section properties propagate on every selection and Run; a full reconcile (including element removal) runs on explicit Save or Sync with base.

docs.title: Construction sequences
docs.text: A construction sequence is an ordered chain of phases. Each phase adds elements (and optionally removes provisional supports), then applies its own load cases as an increment. The analysis is incremental: locked-in internal forces from earlier phases are carried forward, so a member built later does not attract load that was already resisted before it existed.

docs.title: Defining phases
docs.text:
Each phase is defined by a set of Operations — ordered steps that add or remove elements, supports, or load cases. Operations are composed in the Sequences tab of the Variants Workspace.

Two complementary ways to build the element sets:

  • Construction stages — assign each bar element a stage number (select elements, then use Assign to stage k in the Sequences tab). Phase k then activates all elements with stage ≤ k; growth is monotone by construction. A stage-slider in the toolbar lets you preview the geometry at each stage.
  • Scenes — use named canvas selections (Scene menu) as phase templates. From scenes… in the tab generates phases from an ordered list of scenes, either cumulative (each phase adds the next scene) or exact.

docs.title: Running a sequence
docs.text:
Sequences appear in the analysis cases drop-down in the toolbar alongside normal linear and modal cases. Select a sequence case and press Run (F5) as usual. Each phase is solved incrementally and its results are stored. After solving, use the phase selector in the toolbar to navigate phase by phase and view displacements, internal forces and reactions for that increment.

The displacement method is a view setting, not a solver setting:

  • Increment — shows the Δu of the selected phase only.
  • Cumulative — shows the running total u₀ + Δu up to and including the selected phase.

docs.title: Provisional supports and release
docs.text: A phase can reference a support set (defined in the Support sets tab) to install provisional supports such as props or shores. When a subsequent phase drops that support set, the accumulated reaction is automatically converted into an equivalent release load applied to the remaining structure, so the redistribution is captured correctly. Set Release supports to off on a phase to suppress this (the reaction disappears without redistribution).

docs.title: Sequences in the analysis flow
docs.text:
Each construction sequence appears as an Analysis Case of type Sequence in the Analysis Cases panel (shown as read-only). This means:

  • sequences appear in the view drop-down alongside normal cases and combinations (order: analysis cases → sequences → combinations);
  • the Analysis Cases panel shows a Status column (solved / pending) for all cases, including sequences;
  • sequences are included in the Python script export — re-running the exported script rebuilds the full model including all phases and operations.

docs.title: Python script export
docs.text:
File → Export as Python script… (or File → Script editor…) exports the entire model — including variants, support sets, variant combinations, and construction sequences with all their phases and operations — as a runnable Python script. The script uses the public xdfem2d API, so it can be edited and re-run to rebuild a modified version of the model.

Variant models with their own loads and cases are exported as nested helper functions. Construction sequences export their Operation list verbatim and re-resolve the cached phase state (active_elements, applied_cases, case_factors) via resolve_phase_state so the round-trip is exact.

docs.title: How variants and sequences relate
docs.text:
Both features share the staged construction concept — restricting the active geometry to a subset and applying loads incrementally. The key difference is time:

  • A variant is a parallel scenario, solved from scratch independently of the others. There is no inherited state between variants.
  • A construction sequence is time-ordered: each phase inherits the locked-in forces of all previous phases. Removing an element or support releases its accumulated force into the remaining structure.

Both can reference the same support sets, and sequences can be built from the same scenes used to define variant active-element sets.
